Netflix is set to report quarterly earnings after market close on Tuesday as the media industry faces consolidation , spinouts and intensified competition.
Here's how Netflix is expected to perform for the period ended Sept. 30, according to estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:
Last week, Netflix said it was laying off about 6% of employees, or roughly 1,000 workers, and that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria was departing from that role.
The changes come as Netflix faces stagnating viewership and growing competition from the likes of YouTube. At the same time that streaming subscriber additions have slowed in recent years, advertising has once again become a major revenue driver for media companies.
With the help of its cheaper, ad-supported tier, Netflix continues to post solid profits and remains the biggest player in the streaming realm.
On Tuesday, Netflix announced new features for advertisers that it says will help better connect brands to the right audiences and measure the impact of their ads.
However, the company's stock has fallen about 40% in the past year, and executives have been publicly exploring new avenues for growth.

articles.title_orig: Salesforce deepens AI bets with $5.66 billion Braze deal
articles.title_zh: Salesforce deepens AI bets with $5.66 billion Braze deal
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Salesforce slipped roughly 1% on Tuesday morning, after the company announced an agreement to buy customer engagement platform Braze for about $5.66 billion.
Under the deal, holders of Braze Class A common stock will get $47.50 in cash per share. The transaction is expected to close in fiscal 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals, according to a Salesforce blog .
Braze shares closed at $30.04 on Monday. The stock skyrocketed more than 50% on Tuesday after a brief halt premarket following the news. The company makes artificial intelligence marketing tools to manage customer data and messaging.
"Salesforce shares our commitment to marketers, and we'll continue building as Braze and investing in the Braze community of customers and partners who built this company with us," Bill Magnuson, CEO of Braze, said in a statement. "Salesforce's platform will help us innovate faster and together we'll help marketers around the world build deeper, more lasting relationships with their customers."
The latest deal comes just months after Salesforce announced it would buy AI customer service platform Fin for about $3.6 billion, in a move meant to bolster the company's agentic AI offerings for enterprises.
In August, Salesforce and Anthropic announced an expanded partnership , including a new plugin called "Claudeforce" with pre-built sales skills for salespeople to better compose emails, update records and more with the frontier lab's model.

AUBURN — State health inspectors with the Maine Center for Disease Control & Prevention have lifted the imminent health hazard warning and cleared China Wok in Auburn to reopen. The owners plan to reopen on Wednesday at 11 a.m.
A grease fire June 22 forced the closure and led to the discovery of mice droppings in the restaurant at 730 Center St. It has remained closed since.
The owners, Nai and Yan Zhao, have been working with the state and private contractors to repair the damage to the fire suppression hood in the kitchen, and have also been working with a pest control company to eliminate any activity and comply with state health regulations.
Through their daughter, the Zhaos said nothing like this has ever happened to them before, and that not working for the past four months has them looking forward to reopening for all their customers.
Nai Zhao, the father, suffered burns on his hand when oil in one of the woks became hot enough to ignite. Fire spread to the hood/exhaust system, but the Zhaos said the fire suppression system did not engage until the Auburn Fire Department manually triggered it.
The Zhaos bought the business in 2017 from a relative and have worked in the restaurant business for 23 years, paying to send their three daughters to college. One is a senior in college, another a freshman, and the third daughter is in high school.
China Wok halted dine-in seating during the COVID-19 pandemic as all restaurants did, and never resumed seated service. It will continue to be takeout orders only.
China Wok will be open Wednesday and Thursday 11 a.m.-9 p.m., Friday and Saturday 11 a.m.-10 p.m., Sunday and Monday 11 a.m.-9 p.m., and is closed Tuesdays.

articles.title_orig: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
articles.title_zh: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral.
The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 153 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said.
A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF.
The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011.
South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border.
Despite a partial arms embargo on Sudan, foreign countries have been supplying both the army and the RSF with drones and they are increasingly becoming the weapon of choice in the conflict.
The war has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, killed hundreds of thousands of people and forced more than 14 million from their homes.
"We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services," UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Monday .
The rising use of armed drones came as 20 million people faced acute hunger, with a rising risk of famine in parts of the western region of Darfur and Greater Kordofan, he said.
Greater Kordofan comprises three states  and is a vital axis linking Darfur, controlled by the RSF, to the capital, Khartoum, now in army hands.
The wave of drone attacks started on Sunday evening and, according to the Sudan War Observatory, it is likely they were launched from the army-held city of Kadugli in South Kordofan state.
A truck carrying around 200 mourners which had travelled from an area north of Abyei was hit as it arrived in the town of Al-Dabab in West Kordofan, the monitoring group said.
Sources told the group that 145 people were killed and a tent where mourners at the funeral had gathered was also hit, killing five others. A further 150 people were injured in the attacks, it said.
Army drones also bombed a market in the town of Al-Mujlad in West Kordofan on the same evening, according to the Sudan War Observatory, which said the exact number of deaths and injuries were not yet known.
Sudan's army has not responded to the allegation it carried out these strikes, but said it did not attack civilians even if they believed there were RSF fighters amongst them.
The attack in Abyei, which borders West Kordofan, took place on Monday around 11:30 local time (09:30 GMT) targeting Amiet Market around 10km (six miles) from Abyei town, the region's Information Minister Yohana Akol Ngor told Radio Tamazuj, which broadcasts from the Netherlands to audiences on the Sudan-South Sudan border.
On Tuesday, the minister confirmed to the Associated Press and Reuters that the death toll had risen from 73 to 153 people.
"It is a horrible and shocking situation," AP quotes him as saying.
BBC Verify has studied satellite images that show extensive burnt buildings in the north-east corner of Amiet Market, which is also known in Arabic as Al-Na'am Market. Older images from the area show it is usually full of trucks.
It has also verified footage filmed near the market that shows a large plume of smoke, at least one petrol tanker and someone talking about five missiles being fired. Another verified video shows two massive, separate fires coming from buildings near that section of the market.
"The market was completely destroyed. The bombing spread terror and fear among the local population," market trader Fadlallah Adam Hamouda told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily.
Another trader told the BBC the attack had come as shock as UN peacekeepers have been in Abyei since 2011 - with more than 2,800 uniformed personnel currently deployed.
"Our area is a weapons-free zone under United Nations protection, yet it was targeted by drones," he said.
"The attack caused extensive material damage after the fuel market was struck, sparking a massive fire that spread to nearby homes."
Earlier, Ngor told Reuters that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes.
On Monday, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said it had also received people wounded in the attack at Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town.
"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted. We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," MSF's Christian Lindauer, the charity's manager at the hospital, said in a statement.
Meanwhile, a drone strike near the airport in Khartoum on Monday has killed four people, including three children, the AFP news agency reports, quoting a medical source.
It also cited a military source as saying air defences in the Sudanese capital had downed several other drones launched by the RSF towards the airport.
Fighting in Kordofan, a strategic area rich in gold and oil, has intensified over the last year after the army regained control of Khartoum from the RSF.

articles.title_orig: China-Laos air base could be another Southeast Asian forward outpost for Beijing
articles.title_zh: China-Laos air base could be another Southeast Asian forward outpost for Beijing
articles.content_orig:
A new joint military training facility in Laos could give Beijing a lasting foothold in mainland Southeast Asia even without an immediate boost to its combat power, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
Beijing and Vientiane opened a joint support and training center and an aviation academy at Ban Keun, about 50 kilometers north of the Lao capital, on Sept. 29. Beijing says the facility will train Lao air force pilots and it will be maintained by both countries.
The airfield, once complete, would be China’s second joint military outpost in Southeast Asia, after a Chinese-funded expansion of Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base opened in April of last year. The facility at Ream, despite its official designation as a dual-use facility, has seen a regular rotation of Chinese naval vessels.
The joint facility in Laos could allow China to deepen military ties, familiarize personnel with overseas operations and lay the groundwork for a larger presence, Joseph Kristanto, a research analyst at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, told RFA.
“Ultimately, I think the more important question is not simply whether Ban Keun could accommodate Chinese military aircraft, but whether Beijing intends to develop the facility into a sustained operational hub,” he said.
China’s Defense Ministry said in an announcement that the facility would be maintained by both countries and was “not directed against any third party.” It said its construction and use complied with domestic and international law and would strengthen military cooperation and support regional peace and stability.
Laos’ state news agency KPL reported that officials from both countries described the project at the opening ceremony as the product of cooperation based on mutual respect and equality. The facility would develop Lao military pilots’ practical skills, it said.
The KPL report also said both sides pledged to expand cooperation through joint training and exercises, personnel development and humanitarian assistance. Neither that report nor the Chinese announcement specified how many Chinese military personnel would work at Ban Keun, how long they would remain or the conditions governing Chinese aircraft deployments.
Satellite imagery analysis provided to RFA suggests some construction continued after the opening of the joint airfield. But its future military significance will depend on more than its physical completion, including the extent of Chinese access and the frequency and nature of activities there, Kristanto said.
China already operates military facilities on disputed features in the South China Sea. Ban Keun could extend its overseas presence inland, offering opportunities to build closer ties with the Lao military and gain experience operating from a foreign facility, he said.
The airfield’s immediate military advantages are less clear, analysts said. China has airbases in its own southern territory closer to the South China Sea, raising questions about what additional operations an inland facility in Laos would enable.
In satellite imagery of the airfield during its opening, eight aircraft are visible. Private satellite imagery analyst Jacob Bogle told RFA they were K-8, also known as JL-8, light attack and training aircraft.
Examining an Oct. 7 image, he identified what he thought was one remaining aircraft, while cautioning that the image was blurry. He suggested the others had likely moved into hangars, although their locations could not be established from that observation.
Bogle also identified what appeared to be workshops and temporary construction infrastructure beside the southern end of the runway.
“So while the runway and main buildings are completed, it looks like there is still some minor work that is being finished,” he said.
The imagery does not establish who owns or operates the aircraft. Both China and Laos operate the K-8 type, according to analysts cited by Reuters.
But a Lao military officer, while downplaying concerns over increased Chinese military presence in Southeast Asia, confirmed to RFA that at least some of the fighter jets at the facility are Chinese.
“It is a pilot training airport. A group of people are envious that Laos has a flight training center, yet Laos has never complained about neighboring countries hosting U.S. air bases,” said the officer on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak on such matters.
“When Laos built Ban Keun Airport for pilot training, some people overreacted. Naturally, Chinese officials brought their own fighter jets, given that it is a joint Lao-Chinese operation,” he said.
Bogle said it was too early to determine China’s future position at Ban Keun, but that the facility warranted monitoring.
Kristanto said operating combat aircraft from Laos would require substantial investment in fuel storage, maintenance facilities, munitions, air defense and other supporting infrastructure.
“At present, I see little evidence that Ban Keun offers a decisive operational advantage over China’s existing facilities,” he said.
Such limitations do not rule out a broader role in the future. Ban Keun could theoretically support intelligence gathering, surveillance, logistics or forward aircraft deployments if the necessary infrastructure and access arrangements were established, he said.
A sustained Chinese military presence in Laos could add another consideration for neighboring Vietnam, which already faces China across its northern land border and contests Beijing’s claims in the South China Sea.
China’s expansive maritime claims overlap with the exclusive economic zones of Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia. Vietnam also claims the Paracel and Spratly island groups, where competing sovereignty claims are distinct from disputes over rights to surrounding waters. China controls the Paracels, while several governments occupy features in the Spratlys.
In 2016, an international arbitral tribunal rejected China’s claims to the entire South China Sea based on its controversial nine-dash line, which surrounds the whole sea. This claim was seen to exceed what Beijing could legally claim under the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Beijing rejected the decision, and has continued to assert its claims over areas that are within the exclusive economic zones of the other claimants.
China has strengthened this position through island-building and military infrastructure, including runways, surveillance equipment and air defenses on occupied reefs. Those facilities support a wider maritime presence in waters where rival claimants seek to protect fishing grounds, energy resources and access to their outposts.
Ban Keun would introduce a different geographic consideration for Hanoi, potentially bringing Chinese military activity to its western side as well.
Bogle argued that facilities in Laos and Cambodia, together with China’s South China Sea bases, had effectively encircled Vietnam.
Kristanto was more cautious. Vietnam would have to account for the possibility of a Chinese military presence beyond its northern border and the South China Sea, he said, but Ban Keun’s inland location and China’s existing airbases limit its immediate operational value.
“For now, I would characterize Ban Keun as a potentially important strategic foothold rather than a major shift in the regional military balance.”
China’s involvement at Cambodia’s Ream naval base shows why a facility’s use over time can be more revealing than its designation as a joint training center, the analysts said.
China financed an expansion of Ream, on Cambodia’s southern coast, where its joint support and training center opened in April 2025. Cambodia maintains that Chinese personnel and warships are not permanently based there.
An analysis published in May 2025 by the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative documented Chinese naval vessels rotating through Ream after their initial arrival in December 2023.

articles.title_orig: If Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catch
articles.title_zh: If Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catch
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk said on Monday that he will give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year.
He appeared to suggest the gift could land in Trump Accounts — thanking Brad Gerstner, an architect of the program, for "helping enable this" in a comment on X . Posts from the White House and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also referenced Musk's gift as benefiting Trump Accounts.
But if the shares are distributed through the new investment accounts for children, the gift could come with significant strings attached.
Musk's announcement comes weeks after the U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out guidelines for stock donations to Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts. Those include restrictions on selling donated stock: Children who receive it generally cannot sell for five years, even if the company runs into financial trouble.
Treasury's temporary regulations, subject to revision after public comment, aim to encourage stock gifts. But they also give donors unusual influence over children's investments, according to lawyers and philanthropic experts who spoke with CNBC.
In the broader world of charitable giving, donors can typically express preferences about how their gifts are managed, but the receiving organization or trustee retains final authority, said Carolyn Schenck, an attorney and former national fraud counsel at the IRS.
Under the new Trump Account rules, however, it's "the donor that's dictating the terms of the gift," she said.
Representatives for Musk, Gerstner and the Treasury Department did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment on the proposed gift.
According to the Treasury, about 70 million Trump Accounts have been created, including more than 60 million through a recent auto-enrollment effort . Trump Accounts are available to all children with U.S. citizenship under age 18 with valid Social Security numbers.
Musk would be the second philanthropist to publicly announce a stock pledge to Trump Accounts: SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell pledged earlier this summer to use the Trump Account program to gift some 2 million shares . That gift has not yet been distributed.
Trump Account beneficiaries do not have the latitude to sell under circumstances that other investors might otherwise.
Under the new rules, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17. Before then, early sales are permitted only in limited circumstances, such as certain corporate transitions or when the stock is formally delisted from a national securities exchange — not when financial or legal problems emerge that might prompt an investor to sell.
"Giving families more choices and more ability to hold the assets that they think are best for them and their kids' future ... would be a good thing," said Adam Michel, director of tax policy studies at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank. "But this is not really that, because you have no choice in the asset that is being deposited into your child's account, and then you also have no ability to sell it for the five-year holding period."
The temporary regulations also mandate that if any gifted stock is sold too early, the trustee must purchase the same number and class of shares "as soon as practicable."
This increases beneficiaries' risk of loss if the share price rises before the trustee repurchases the stock, according to Schenck. Beneficiaries would ultimately bear that cost.
"If the fiduciary makes an investment mistake, then the focus is typically restoring value to the beneficiary. But here, the focus seems to be restoring the specific security itself," said Schenck, who left the IRS in 2025 for law firm Caplin & Drysdale.
CNBC has learned the buyback provision is intended to quickly correct trading errors, though the regulations do not explicitly state that purpose or limit the requirement to accidental sales.
The temporary regulations cite donor interests. According to the text, "Donors are attracted by the hope that a stock contribution with a five-year holding period may lead recipients and their families to feel that they have a stake in the fate of the corporation."
Restricting sales virtually eliminates the risk for donors and their companies that Trump Account recipients will sell gifted shares en masse, liquidating a large enough position to depress share prices, according to Jane Ditelberg, chief tax strategist at Northern Trust.
"Certainly, for people who have highly concentrated wealth in a company, and the assets are sitting in their own personal pockets, this makes it a lot easier to give," she said.
Generally speaking, donors can get a bigger tax benefit by gifting appreciated stock to charity than donating cash, as they can claim the charitable deduction and avoid capital gains tax on the gains.
A Treasury official told CNBC that the rules are intended to build long-term wealth for children, especially in lower-income families, and encourage donations. "The major donors we've engaged are motivated by a desire to help children build generational wealth and get a head start on their financial future," the official said in a written statement.
Treasury has said it is in discussions with Trump Accounts donors ranging from "small to mega," but has not identified additional stock pledges since Shotwell's July announcement.
CNBC has identified fewer than a dozen pledges from philanthropists, though about four dozen major employers have committed to seed accounts for their employees' children.
In documents explaining the temporary rules, Treasury pointed to Michael and Susan Dell's $6.25 billion cash pledge and unspecified "similar donations," while acknowledging uncertainty about whether that level of giving will continue. "It is unclear whether this level of giving can be sustained in the long run or whether it is concentrated as Trump accounts are launching," the text states.
Trump Account funds generally may be invested only in low-cost index funds and exchange-traded funds. In the temporary regulations, the Treasury said directly contributed stock is different because it doesn't use account funds for the purchase.
But Ditelberg said a court could conclude that requiring an account to retain individual shares is still an investment decision — an argument that may carry more weight after the Supreme Court's overturning of Chevron deference . Because of the 2024 ruling, courts no longer have to defer to federal agencies' interpretations of statutes when the language is unclear.
"These accounts are going to have to stay invested in those stocks, and the question is whether that's directly contradicting the terms of the statute," she said. "I can't tell you how a court would rule, but I could say there's room for a challenge here."
Ditelberg added that state law grants the right to disclaim an asset. She said it's unclear how the Trump Account donation procedures would accommodate that right.
Schenck noted that Treasury has broad authority to set the terms of Trump Accounts, and it is Treasury — not the original stock donor — that formally requires the shares to be held.
The arrangement also differs from traditional charitable giving. For example, donors who contribute stock to donor-advised funds can recommend how the assets are managed, but the sponsoring charity retains ultimate control, including the authority to sell the shares. This is required to meet the IRS's legal standards for taking a tax deduction on a charitable contribution.
"A key principle is that the charity must have genuine control over the donated assets, including the ability to determine when to sell them, for the gift to qualify as a completed charitable contribution," said Gil Nusbaum, chief administrative and legal officer of National Philanthropic Trust.
Experts say the broader question is whether Treasury's approach aligns with the law Congress enacted.

articles.content_orig:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky says intelligence on early warning systems for Russian strikes "works now" , and that he is "thankful" to the US
The US has previously denied limiting intelligence sharing . Today, the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected accusations Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence
During a news conference in Oslo after meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Zelensky also says he is "ready for negotiations" and calls for trilateral talks with the US and Russia - here's what we heard

Witkoff will meet with Russian leadership tomorrow and "exchange ideas", Norway's PM Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re says at the conference
The talks come amid deteriorating relations between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump
Edited by Manish Pandey and Matt Spivey
Trump was asked by a reporter in the Oval Office about the war in Ukraine
We have just heard from US President Donald Trump, who says the US has given "tremendous" amounts to Ukraine but received nothing back in return.
Speaking from the Oval Office, following an announcement about fraud, the US president says it is time for Ukraine to end the war.
He describes the hatred been Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelensky as being "tremendous", saying this may be the reason they have been unable to reach a deal.
"We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss," Trump says.
As we reported earlier, President Zelensky said in the press conference that he is "thankful" to the US as intelligence on Russian strikes "works now".
Zelensky's adviser Serhii Beskrestnov last week told the BBC that lives had been lost in Ukraine because Kyiv was at the time not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks.
White House officials have said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the two countries.
Earlier today, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected as "scandalous" accusations that Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence.
Zelensky told reporters this evening that the early warning systems are important to the Ukrainian people and children as it shows when attacks are incoming.

Zelensky also said restrictions on Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing. He earlier said speed limits had been imposed on Starlink terminals, and that Kyiv had not been told about this in advance.
Internet service Starlink allows Ukraine to effectively guide drones to Russian targets and to protect Ukrainian skies.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky then says he is "thankful" to the US as intelligence on Russian strikes "works now".
He adds that early warning systems are important to the Ukrainian people and says "we are thankful to American side now it works, it is great".
The US has previously denied limiting intelligence sharing.
A question is asked about why special envoy Steve Witkoff is not present, to which Norwegian PM Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re says the news conference is for political leaders.

He responds by saying Ukraine wants to push as quickly as possible to end this war, and that they are ready for negotiations.
"Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks," he says, adding that he hopes their partners - including the US - will help them in ending the war.

Finnish President Alexander Stubb is up next. He says those present at the talks made "genuine progress" on two levels: in the "big picture" and the "short-term".
He says they "found some elements of peace" in the big picture, and those ideas will be taken to St Petersburg tomorrow, as well as key elements on security and the economy.
In the short-term, he says they discussed air defence, energy installations and partial ceasefires, adding that he feels the leaders are "on the same page".
"In my experience, peace requires patience. But unfortunately war does not wait. People are dying every and each day... I think today was a step in the right direction," he adds.
Now the leaders are moving on to questions from reporters.
Zelensky continues by saying Ukraine "immediately" supported the US proposal for an energy ceasefire, but Russia "responded by continuing its attacks".
He says he wants US representatives to take ideas discussed for a potential peaceful solution to the Russians.
The Ukrainian president says one of the ideas is to move towards a potential trilateral meeting between leaders.
He adds that Witkoff is going to Russia tomorrow: "Let's see what Putin has to say."
Zelensky finishes his remarks by thanking everyone who stands with Ukraine and peace.
We're now hearing from Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky, and he begins by saying it's "important that we keep talking at all levels, and work together on decisions needed to end this war".
He says he has been holding "important talks" with Ukraine's partners in the US and Europe.
Zelensky confirms he had a "good conversation" with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio - and says he appreciated his willingness to help and find solutions to the issues faced by Ukraine.
Ukraine wants peace more than anyone, Zelensky says, and the decision to keep the killing going, is Russia's choice, and Russia's alone.
StÃ¸re continues and says US special envoy Steve Witkoff will fly tomorrow to St Petersburg in Russia, to meet with the Russian leadership and "exchange ideas" from today's meeting and the proposals that have been discussed.
He adds this could "possibly pave the way for a meeting at leaders level", and says that the issues spoken about today include Ukraine's security, a prosperity plan after the war, territory and sanctions.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re begins the news conference by saying Norway is supporting Ukraine's "legitimate defence against military aggression".
He also thanks Finnish President Alexander Stubb for his work, saying he and the president are "like-minded".
StÃ¸re acknowledges US special envoy Steve Witkoff was in attendance at today's meeting, with Jared Kushner also present via video link.
He says he believes "peace is possible and necessary" for Ukraine, Europe and the entire world, describing today's talks as "good and constructive".

articles.title_orig: Two men rearrested on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service in RAF Fairford incident
articles.title_zh: Two men rearrested on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service in RAF Fairford incident
articles.content_orig:
British counterterrorism police said Tuesday they have rearrested two men in their investigation into last month’s incident at RAF Fairford in England, where US B-1 bombers were based.
A 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national were rearrested on suspicion of assisting Iran’s foreign intelligence service, police said in a statement.
“So far seven men have been arrested in connection with our investigation,” Laurence Taylor, a senior counterterrorism police officer, said in a statement. “As a result of the ongoing efforts of our officers, earlier today two of those men were re-arrested for offences relating to Section 3 of the National Security Act — assisting a foreign intelligence service.”
“This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement,” Taylor added. The other five men are currently out on bail. Police have not released the names of any of them.
In late September, British authorities announced the initial arrest of five men “on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act” and explosives offenses near RAF Fairford, a British air base long used by the US Air Force. Army bomb disposal units and police officers swarmed the area and evacuated civilian homes around the base.
Earlier this month, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that the suspected plot targeting RAF Fairford was “almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard.” Iran has firmly rejected the accusations.
US President Donald Trump praised the arrests at the time, telling reporters that the US had worked with Britain and that the men arrested were planning to do “big damage” to RAF Fairford.
“We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” Trump said. US intelligence had tracked planning by Iranian groups to target US assets at the base weeks ahead of any arrests, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.
Residents around RAF Fairford also may have tipped authorities off. One resident, who asked to remain anonymous, told CNN that she had called police after seeing three vans surrounded by eight to 10 masked men blocking her driveway.
In an interview with Sky News, British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting thanked the woman for making the emergency call. He mentioned that she had only a “partial picture” and offered no further details.
Developments at the base did not end there. Days after the initial arrests, the US moved all of its long-range bombers from RAF Fairford following an unspecified threat, a knowledgeable source said.
At the time, Trump and Vice President JD Vance hinted that a threat against US assets had prompted the move.
“I think we can say that — I mean, they didn’t fly out by accident,” Trump said. “There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy, we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit.”
Vance said the move was made “out of an abundance of caution,” suggesting it was a response to a potential threat from Iran even as he declined to detail the specific concerns.
As of Tuesday, none of the US bombers had returned to Fairford.
This is a developing story and will be updated.
CNN’s Piper Hudspeth Blackburn, Zachary Cohen and Jennifer Hansler contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Student Protesters in France Have a Strange New Slogan. What Does It Mean?
articles.title_zh: Student Protesters in France Have a Strange New Slogan. What Does It Mean?
articles.content_orig:
(Photo by: Vincent Koebel/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
“Mamadou” was clearly itching to get straight to business when he sent a message on Snapchat to one of the young organizers of the recent student protests that have seen high schools across France blockaded and thousands of teens taking to the streets to demand more funding for education. The “student,” who sported an Algerian and Senegalese flag alongside his name on Snapchat, wanted to break some things — everything, in fact. And to be added to the group where such delinquency might be discussed.
“Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres,” his message begins, “In the name of God, it is the darkness.” The message continues in a mashup of North African Arabic and French slang that I will try to reproduce as faithfully to the tone as possible here: “When’s the blockade I swear my homies. We’re gonna break everything. Add me to the blockade group, thank you,” followed by two Algerian flag emojis.
The short message was so full of absurdities, anachronisms and racist assumptions that the recipient knew at once it wasn’t from a fellow student. It was, they suspected, from the police, trying to infiltrate their organizing network and conjuring their own ideas of how kids talked and behaved to do it. Later reporting from La Provence indicated they weren’t too far off: The geolocation of the original message indicated that it likely came from a police station in Aix-en-Provence, the news site reported.
Rather than dismiss it, the students have transformed the nonsense phrase “Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres” into its own shibboleth — and something akin to the great Steve Buscemi “How do you do, fellow kids” meme of the 2010s. It has appeared on placards and banners at protests across the country; student leaders are using it as a rallying cry; even Greta Thunberg invoked it in a recent video supporting the movement.
Beyond the meme, however, is the reality of the way the French state views its young citizens , particularly those of Arab, Maghrebi and African descent. The issue that drove students to the streets — underfunded schools where buildings are falling apart and teacher absenteeism is rampant — impacts Black and Arab neighborhoods at higher rates. As does aggressive policing . A 2017 survey by the independent public institution Defenseurs des Droits found that young men who were perceived as Black, Arab or Maghrebi were 20 times more likely to be stopped by police for an identity check than others; a 2024 update to that survey found that the same group was 12 times more likely to have such an encounter escalate to a pat-down, search or trip to a police station.
After weeks of relatively calm protests from students, met by ample tear gas from the police, “the darkness” arrived over the weekend. France saw rioting and looting alongside an estimated 550,000-800,000 people on the streets, who hitched their grievances about the cost of living and social mobility to the students’ cause. At least 2,400 people were arrested. In Saint-Etienne, a 17-year-old lost his hand after being hit by a crowd-control grenade. The far right was quick to turbocharge its impending presidential campaign by laying the blame on “immigrants,” though internal assessments by the government point to far-left factions and opportunistic criminals who met a lack of anticipation and preparation by the police.
The cost of the protests — politically, socially, financially — will be determined in the coming weeks and months. But the underlying disconnect between the state and its rising generation will continue long after the shattered glass is swept up and the charred cars towed away.

articles.title_orig: China built more than twice naval tonnage of US in 2024-25: Euronaval
articles.title_zh: China built more than twice naval tonnage of US in 2024-25: Euronaval
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — China built more than twice the naval tonnage of the United States in the 2024-25 period, narrowing the gap between the two countries’ navies, according to the World Defense Shipbuilding report published by Euronaval ahead of the 2026 edition of the naval defense show.
The combined tonnage of combat ships built by China in the two years through to December 2025 amounted to 636,208 tons, compared to 270,509 tons for the United States, according to data compiled by Flottes de Combat and French maritime industry association Gican.
China accounted for more than a third of the global naval tonnage constructed in 2024-25, based on the Euronaval report. U.S. lawmakers and congressional researchers have warned that China’s greater shipbuilding capacity, combined with delays and bottlenecks in U.S. naval shipbuilding, could hurt America’s ability to keep up with Beijing’s expanding fleet.
“We are seeing a fairly substantial expansion of naval forces, and consequently of shipbuilding,” said Philippe Missoffe, the general director of Gican, in a press briefing here on Tuesday. “We’re seeing an increase in power capabilities, particularly nuclear-powered attack submarines for example.”
Global naval construction overall was booming in the period, with 1.47 million tons of combat vessels built in 2024-25, compared with 959,671 tons in the prior two years. The value of global naval construction amounted to $123.9 billion, climbing from $81.8 billion in 2022-23.
The value of Chinese combat-vessel construction was US$43.5 billion in the latest two-year period, compared with $26.8 billion for the U.S., the report said.
China has reversed roles from 2022-2023, when production of the country’s naval yards amounted to 202,520 tons, compared with 245,703 tons for the U.S., according to the previous edition of the shipbuilding report published in 2024.
The U.S. fleet of combat vessels of more than 200 tons amounted to 3.11 million tons as of Jan. 1, 2026, compared to 1.44 million tons for China’s fleet, the report showed, That compares with 3.22 million tons for the U.S. and 1.3 million tons for China two years earlier.
Russia was in third place in terms of naval construction in 2024-25, with 149,056 tons built, followed by India with 76,430 tons and Italy with 53,700 tons. Turkey, France, Japan, South Korean and Romania rounded out the top 10 of naval builders.
The four-day Euronaval show, the world’s biggest maritime-defense exhibition, is set to kick of in Paris on Nov. 3. The number of exhibitors will be more than 40% higher than in 2024, according to the organizers.
Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

articles.title_orig: Don't Put Your Phone In The TSA Bin — Do This Instead
articles.title_zh: Don't Put Your Phone In The TSA Bin — Do This Instead
articles.content_orig:
Let's be honest, TSA bins are just gross.
After years of traveling with a small arsenal of tech — usually a phone, iPad, laptop and a portable gaming console — I like to think I'm pretty efficient when it comes to taking them out of my bag at TSA checkpoints . But it's still a pain to hastily repack them while also putting on my shoes, grabbing my belt and just trying not to hold up the line of people behind me in the process.
Going through airport security can be a little stressful, and the last thing you're probably thinking about is how to properly stow away your loose items in the plastic bins. But we should all be a little more mindful of that, especially when it comes to our phones. For one thing, chucking your phone with all your other stuff is an easy way to lose track of it as you try to rush to your next flight.
But there's also another important factor to consider about why we shouldn't leave our phones, the one device we constantly touch and put up to our face, unprotected. And it has to do with basic hygiene.
I've never worked as a TSA officer, nor do I know anyone who has, but I'm fairly confident that the bins are rarely cleaned. I can understand why: When you think about the hundreds of thousands of people who go through US airports on a daily basis, and how understaffed the TSA can be, it'd take a lot of time and manpower to disinfect the bins and feed them back to the security lines.
But you don't have to be a germaphobe to realize how grimy those things can get. Tons of people touch them, they often have dirty shoes inside and you never know if someone is sick and placing their infected gear in there, too. Some studies even show that they can be a haven for viruses and bacteria . So if you want to avoid having any last-minute travel companions, you need to make sure your phone isn't in direct contact with the bins.
Before you get to the X-ray machine, you can tuck your phone away in your carry-on or in the pocket of a jacket that you place inside a bin. Same advice goes for any other small items you have to pull out for TSA, like wallets and keys. And of course, make sure to wash your hands or have some hand sanitizer ready to use when you're through with security.
Contamination is harder to avoid with larger electronics, as most TSA checkpoints still require you to take laptops, tablets and handheld game consoles out of your bags and into a separate bin (unless the line you're in has a CT scanner that lets you leave everything inside). There isn't much you can do there, but at the very least, they should all have their own cases that protect them from the elements.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street rises with investors rotating into healthcare and value stocks
articles.title_zh: Wall Street rises with investors rotating into healthcare and value stocks
articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose on Tuesday as a number of upbeat earnings reports and a drop in oil prices overshadowed recent pressure seen among artificial intelligence-related stocks.
The blue-chip index gained 471 points, or 0.9%, while the S&P 500 added 0.3%. The Nasdaq Composite traded up 0.1%.
Shares of industrial and safety products producer 3M offered a boost to the Dow, jumping more than 5% following better-than-expected earnings results and a full-year guidance raise . Shares of aerospace and defense company Northrop Grumman also advanced more than 5% after it posted an earnings beat.
Meanwhile, oil prices pulled back from earlier gains, helping investor sentiment. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were last down less than 1% at around $103 per barrel, while Brent crude futures fell about 1% to roughly $108 a barrel. The moves in oil, which added to the declines in Treasury yields , come as traders continued to monitor developments in the Middle East.
The market has been weighed down as of late by worries about the sustainability of the AI trade amid debt and demand concerns. In fact, sentiment in tech took a hit earlier in the day after Korean AI firm Elice tumbled more than 30% overnight in its public market debut. Asia-Pacific markets declined Tuesday, after U.S. stocks rose overnight, leading to declines in the South Korean market.
However, AI-related stocks staged a bit of a comeback as the session went on. Micron Technology , Sandisk and Advanced Micro Devices all rose around 1%. Intel climbed more than 1%, while Seagate Technology , was up more than 2%. CoreWeave gained more than 2%.
The S&P 500 finished in positive territory on Monday, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced more than 1%. That marked a rebound from last week's rout, when anxieties around companies borrowing too much money for their AI build-outs intensified.
"For much of this year, the market has been willing to look through higher rates because the growth story, notably that around AI, was strong enough to justify it. Last week, we saw that relationship begin to be tested," said Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion.
"Hyperscalers report over the next few weeks, setting up the next major stress test for the AI trade," he continued. "Guidance around ROI, data center spending and 2027 capex will arguably be more important than the headline earnings figures."
Shares of Netflix were down more than 1% in afternoon trading on Tuesday as investors geared up for the release of its latest quarterly results after the bell.
Analysts surveyed by LSEG are expecting the company to report 82 cents in earnings per share and revenue of $12.87 billion.
The report comes amid a downbeat year for the stock, as it's fallen more than 26%.
— Sean Conlon and Sarah Whitten
Starboard Value CEO, Jeff Smith believes the coming years "is going to be amazing," for value stocks, he told CNBC at the 13D Monitor Active-Passive Investor Summit Tuesday.
It's because companies that use artificial intelligence across their organizations should improve their margins "much faster" from creating greater efficiencies.
His comments come as he sees many value stocks currently trading at low multiples.
"Being able to buy in at that value and be your own catalyst to get them to improve their margins; I think the next, how ever many years, is going to be amazing," Smith said.

Read here for the full list.
TD Cowen upgraded BlackRock to buy from hold on Tuesday, citing the company is ahead of revenue and operating income targets.
TD Cowen's Bill Katz also increased the company's price target to $1,405, a nearly 25% upside from Monday's close.
Katz added that BlackRock has several avenues for organic growth, including in private markets and retirement.
3M shares popped more than 5% after the producer of industrial and safety products posted adjusted earnings of $2.50 per share, more than the LSEG estimate of $2.38 per share.
Shares of GE Aerospace were off 2% after the company reported its third-quarter financials, where the company delivered an earnings and revenue beat.
GE Aerospace reported adjusted earnings of $2.25 per share, compared to analysts polled by LSEG's estimates for $2.01 per share. Revenue also came in above expectations at $13.29 billion.
The company also hiked guidance across various metrics for the full-year, however free cash flow at $2.04 billion was lower than expectations for $2.2 billion, according to StreetAccount.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite began Tuesday's session in the red.
The broad market index fell 0.2% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq pulled back 0.4%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average traded around the flatline.
Investor concerns over CoreWeave 's credit ticked higher on Tuesday, with the spread on its five-year credit default swap rising back up near levels seen on Thursday .
The CDS, which is a way for buyers to pay for protection in case the borrower defaults, last saw spreads over 1,121, which is up 2.22% for the day and more than 17% over the past week. Spreads of 1,000 or greater are generally considered a sign of distress.
Housing starts slumped in September, raising fresh concerns about the state of the real estate market as the Federal Reserve contemplates additional interest rate hikes.
The Commerce Department reported Tuesday that privately owned starts totaled 1.22 million at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate. That was off 5.2% from the August level and well below the Dow Jones consensus for 1.3 million.
Additionally, single-family starts weakened, totaling 859,000, off 4.6% from the prior month.
Building permits issued during the month were slightly better than expected, totaling a seasonally adjusted annualized 1.4 million, against the estimate for 1.39 million. The total was 0.2% below August.

General Motors beat Wall Street's expectations on the top- and bottom-lines as it reported its Q3 2026 earnings, delivering strong results driven by high truck sales and growing subscription revenue
The company raised its free cash flow expectations and narrowed its 2026 full-year guidance.
The Detroit automaker also announced a new multiyear stock buyback of $20 billion, but didn't provide a specific timeframe for the repurchase.
"GM is performing well, and we are working hard to continue our momentum despite growing inflationary pressures through strategic investments in new products and services, and through improved quality and operating efficiency," GM CEO Mary Barra said Tuesday in a letter to shareholders.
GM expects commodity inflation costs to be nearly $2 billion, which was the high end of its previous guidance. The automaker also said the costs of its pullback in all-electric vehicles announced last year were "substantially completed."
GM stock was off roughly 7% during premarket trading despite the beats.
Korean AI firm Elice tumbled more than 30% overnight in its public market debut. Investors recently have been worried about the sustainability of the AI trade, as debt and demand concerns grow .
Shares of Solstice Advanced Materials , which was spun off from Honeywell last year, rose more than 3% after The Financial Times reported, citing sources, that activist Starboard Value had built a stake in the company.
Starboard wants Solstice to cut about $100 million in corporate costs focus on its refrigerants and nuclear businesses, the report said . Solstice shares are up more than 24% year to date.

articles.title_orig: AMD Announces FSR 4.1 for Xbox Series X/S, Z2 Extreme and Z2A Handhelds, RX 6000 GPUs and More
articles.title_zh: AMD Announces FSR 4.1 for Xbox Series X/S, Z2 Extreme and Z2A Handhelds, RX 6000 GPUs and More
articles.content_orig:
Earlier this month AMD senior vice president Jack Huynh told media in South Korea that FSR 4 was coming to more devices, including handhelds - and now that promise has been fulfilled.
Huynh today announced that FSR 4.1 was coming to five new platforms: Radeon RX 6000-series graphics cards; Gorgon Halo and Strix Halo mini PCs and mobile workstations; Gorgon Halo and Strix Halo Ryzen 9 laptops; Z2 Extreme and Z2A handhelds like ROG Xbox Ally devices; and Xbox Series X and Series S.
It's a welcome surprise to see AMD's latest generation upscaler on a huge range of extra devices - even though community modders have been working hard to port the technique to an even longer list of supported platforms.
FSR 4, previously known as Project Redstone, is AMD's first machine learning upscaler and offers a significant visual advantage over its earlier efforts at similar frame-rates - hence the interest in making it available on a wider range of PCs, handhelds and other devices. As well as upscaling and anti-aliasing, the tech also includes frame generation and ray reconstruction, giving it better feature parity with Nvidia's similar DLSS tech.
Huynh's announcement also states that FSR is coming to Vulkan, a graphics API that is the default choice for games that don't use (or want to offer an alternative to) DirectX 12. FSR 3 and earlier supported Vulkan, so it's good to see this limitation redressed - though it's not clear how quickly developers will be able to add FSR 4.1 support to their Vulkan games.
More APUs will get FSR 4.1 support in the future, Huynh claimed, and the announcement video also mentions that AMD's next-gen FSR Diamond will be supported on Xbox's Project Helix " family of devices ".
If you want to use FSR 4.1 on your PC (officially) for the first time, you'll need to install Adrenalin Edition version 26.10.1 . The graphics drivers also add support for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, Star Wars: Galactic Racer and Final Fantasy Resonance.
What do you make of the news? Let me know in the comments below.

articles.title_orig: Ahead of massive IPOs, AI companies are sketching plans to share their wealth
articles.title_zh: Ahead of massive IPOs, AI companies are sketching plans to share their wealth
articles.content_orig:
Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.
As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.
One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.
We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as a wholly-owned LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.
Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.
This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.
In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive: Joel Kaplan leaving Meta after 15 years as policy chief
articles.title_zh: Exclusive: Joel Kaplan leaving Meta after 15 years as policy chief
articles.content_orig:
Joel Kaplan will remain through the 2026 midterms while Dina Powell McCormick and C.J. Mahoney add policy duties
Joel Kaplan, Meta $META 's chief global affairs officer, will leave the company in 2027 after more than 15 years, according to Bloomberg . The news came from a company representative.
Kaplan will stay through the U.S. midterm elections and into 2027 to oversee a transition, according to Axios . That handover will bring in executives who handle external affairs and who span the two major parties, Axios said, with many having joined Meta 's leadership team within the past year.
Kaplan joined Meta in 2011 to oversee U.S. public policy, according to Bloomberg. Earlier in his career, he served on George W. Bush's campaign and later in Bush's administration, and he has long counseled CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Kaplan moved into the top global policy job in the run-up to President Donald Trump's early-2025 return to the White House, according to Bloomberg.
Axios described Kaplan as a former deputy White House chief of staff under Bush who assembled Facebook 's U.S. policy operation from the ground up.
"Joel has worked on virtually every tough issue Meta has faced for more than 15 years," Zuckerberg said in a statement to Axios. "When he arrived, there was no playbook for ensuring our products would be available to the billions of people around the world who now rely on them," Zuckerberg added.
Several executives will absorb Kaplan's responsibilities, according to Axios:
Dina Powell McCormick, Meta 's president and vice chairman, will take responsibility for external affairs on top of her existing duties. She also co-leads Meta Compute, the company's AI infrastructure initiative.
C.J. Mahoney, who became chief legal officer in January, will take on policy responsibilities. He is a former Trump administration trade official and former Microsoft $MSFT general counsel.
Brian Rice, who earlier worked as an aide to then-Secretary of State John Kerry, moved up this year to lead U.S. government affairs.
Tucker Bounds, who once spoke on behalf of the late Sen. John McCain, was named in September as global head of communications and public affairs. He has been with Meta for more than a dozen years, according to Axios.

President Trump said the U.S. is "doing very well with Iran" and he's just deciding how he wants to win the war.
"As you know, we're doing very well with Iran," Mr. Trump said as he took questions from reporters in the Oval Office at an unrelated executive order signing. "We just have to make a final decision of which way do we want to win? Do we want to win the nice way or the not nice way? But we're doing very well."
The war, which Mr. Trump said would take only a few weeks in March, has now dragged on for almost eight months with no apparent end in sight. Iran said on Tuesday it would not return to the negotiating table unless the U.S. drops its sanctions, threats and pressure campaign — an unlikely demand.
The president also discussed Europe not helping the U.S. with the war with Iran, saying, "We don't need any help. But I was testing them."
"I just called individual presidents and prime ministers to ask, would they like to help us? And they said, 'No,'" Mr. Trump said. "I said, 'Well, that's not nice.' You know, we spend hundreds of billions a year on NATO. And they said no."
Iran is taking a hard-line stance on negotiations with the U.S. to end the war, with President Masoud Pezeshkian saying Tuesday there will be no return to talks without a halt to the pressure campaign by the U.S.
Pezeshkian met with representatives from Pakistan, including army chief Asim Munir, on Tuesday. Pakistan has played an integral role as a mediator in peace talks between the U.S. and Iran, including the brief success of the Islamabad Memorandum in June.
"(Pezeshkian) told Pakistan's Field Marshal Asim Munir that US warmongering lies behind regional tensions, including disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz," according to a readout of the meeting from the official Iranian government account on X . "He said Washington must lift its pressures, threats and sanctions before any negotiations."
Those conditions are unlikely to be agreed upon by the U.S., which has stepped up its sanctions , dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, over the past month. President Trump has said the economic pressure campaign has become the main strategy for ending the war.
Pezeshkian also met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran on Tuesday. Iran and Russia have become powerful allies.
Naval mines have halted three tankers attempting to travel the Strait of Hormuz via routes considered illegal by Tehran, Iranian Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday.
"Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," the Guards said in an earlier statement on their official Sepah News website.
The Guards later said in a statement carried by state TV that a third oil tanker "exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz."
The tanker "carrying over 2 million barrels of crude oil, had deactivated all of its radar and navigation systems," the statement added.
Iranian forces have, since the outbreak of the Middle East war, repeatedly targeted ships attempting to pass through Hormuz via a southern, U.S.-approved route close to the Omani coast.
President Trump has said on several occasions that the Strait of Hormuz has been cleared of all mines.
Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, on Tuesday told visiting Pakistani army chief Asim Munir that Tehran will not allow nuclear material to leave the country, according to state TV.
"Not even a tiny bit of enriched nuclear material will leave Iran. Such materials constitute a major asset and national wealth for the Iranian people, intended for use within the country," said Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
"There will be no negotiations until America takes steps to build trust — a process that must begin with the fulfilment of Iran's conditions."
President Trump has made preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon the administration's top priority.
"They can't have a nuclear weapon," Mr. Trump said Monday night at a rally in Kansas. "OK, and they won't. By the way, somebody said you could leave right now. It's true. We can leave right now. They're not going to have a nuclear weapon."

"I wish to draw your immediate attention, as well as that of the members of the Security Council, to the recent brazen existential threats made by the President of the United States regarding the possible use of the GBU-43/B bomb, officially known as the Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), also referred to as the "Mother of All Bombs," against Iran, as well as the renewed threats by the Israeli regime of military aggression and its declared intention to target all of Iran's energy infrastructure," Darzi wrote in his letter, according to state-owned media.
The letter from Darzi asks for Guterres and the head of the U.N. Security Council to convene a meeting and highlights four demands from the 15-country group, which permanently includes the U.S., China, Russia, France and the U.K.
Iran asks for the security council to call upon the U.S. and Israel to end their "unlawful threats" toward Iran; explicitly and unequivocally condemn threats to attack Iran; address threats to regional peace; and ensure accountability and reparations for damage from "wrongful acts committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran."
"Threatening to use the 'MOAB' bomb (the Mother of All Bombs) against Iran's civilian infrastructure and to target all of the country's energy infrastructure constitutes, among other things, a flagrant violation of international law," Darzi wrote.

articles.title_orig: China ramps up cyberattacks for potential election meddling: officials
articles.title_zh: China ramps up cyberattacks for potential election meddling: officials
articles.content_orig:
The Government Service Network (GSN) reported a surge of 185.6 million cyberattacks in July, suggesting that Beijing could be preparing large-scale interference operations ahead of the Nov. 28 elections, government officials said.
Cyberattacks on the network, likely originating in China, spiked between June and last month, the National Security Bureau (NSB) said in a report submitted to the Legislative Yuan for a meeting scheduled for tomorrow.
As of last month, the GSN was attacked 2.58 million times a day on average, and the attacks reported in July exceeded the sum of total cyberattacks in the first quarter this year, the document said.
Cyberattacks exceeded 100 million in three months last year: during the anniversary of President William Lai’s (賴清德) inauguration in April (100 million), in May (about 300 million) and during Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim’s (蕭美琴) visit to Europe in November (about 200 million), it said.
The NSB cannot rule out the possibility that the July attacks are part of Beijing’s plan to meddle in next month’s nine-in-one elections, the report said, adding that the agency had warned of the same in April.
Chinese hackers in the first half of the year targeted academic institutions, telecommunications and defense industry supply chains as part of a long war against Taiwan’s critical infrastructure, it said.
The attacks were aimed at disrupting Taiwan’s ability to govern and direct national defense policy, its collaboration with other governments and the theft of sensitive technology, it said.
Beijing-directed cyberwarfare continues to improve in sophistication and artificial intelligence (AI) technology has been deployed in hacks, it said.
AI is utilized across various stages of a cyberattack, including probing for weaknesses, target seeking, searching for zero-day exploits and malware attacks via e-mail, the report said.
Automation has increased Chinese hackers’ operational tempo and their efficiency in finding gaps in Taiwan’s defenses and identifying targets for infiltration, it said.
Meanwhile, the NSB said it believes that Beijing would leverage technology and human intelligence to craft a strategy to influence next month’s elections, targeting Taiwan’s domestic wedge issues such as energy, food safety and national defense, and using fake polls and reports about the races, and AI-generated content, it said.
Suspicious social media accounts made 2.5 million posts containing controversial or disputed information from January to last month, up 48 percent compared with 1.69 million in the same period last year, the report said.
The method and platform for spreading cognitive warfare posts included content farms, AI-generated video or audio content, and brigading the comment section on platforms, forums and other Web sites, it said.
Facebook and Threads accounted for 68.9 percent and 9 percent respectively of all controversial content from suspicious accounts, it said.
Suspicious posts on Facebook and Threads were up by 25.3 and 4.5 percentage points from last year respectively, indicating China’s increasing preference for using these platforms, the report said.
AI is playing an increasingly prominent role in Beijing’s informational operations, it said.
China’s strategy for manipulating Taiwanese public opinion follows the model of using official outlets to craft narratives, which are then amplified by troll, bot and public relations company-owned accounts, the report said.

articles.content_orig:
@Kittipong Jirasukhanont from PhonlamaiPhoto's Images via Canva, @jamesteohArt via Canva
Now Live: Discover how much upside your favorite stocks could have using TIKR’s new Valuation Model (It’s free) >>>
Nvidia ( NVDA ) is seeing a rush of demand from China.
Two people familiar with the matter told Reuters that ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have ordered more than 3 million RTX PRO 5500 cards. At about $11,400 each, the orders are worth over $35 billion .
The RTX PRO 5500 is a workstation chip, which is less powerful than the H200 and B300 data center chips.
But it is among the most powerful Nvidia chips Chinese buyers can still get. The B300 is not allowed to be sold to Chinese buyers and H200 exports are reviewed case by case.
Nvidia may not be able to fill all the orders. Sources said partners might get only 5% to 10% of what they asked for.
One source said Nvidia could make no more than 3 million cards globally in 2027 and total orders from China have topped 6 million.
Early samples are expected in December and commercial deliveries would start in the first quarter of 2027.
Chinese firms want the cards mainly for inference, which means running trained AI models to answer chatbot requests.
That takes less computing power than training. The older RTX 6000D drew little interest last year and hopes that Washington would allow stronger chips have faded, which makes the new card more appealing.
An Nvidia spokesperson blamed “outdated US export controls” and China’s own limit on US imports.
See analysts’ growth forecasts and price targets for Nvidia stock (It’s free) >>>
For Nvidia stock, the story is about demand more than sales, and the chipmaker has also said it cannot guarantee delivery.
This matters because China has been a lost market. Jensen Huang has said the curbs cut Nvidia’s share of China’s AI data center chip market from a near monopoly to almost nothing.
These orders suggest a sizable market may still exist for less powerful chips.
Nvidia’s outlook does not count on China. On its August call, the company said there is no China data center compute revenue in its forward outlook. So any China sales would be extra upside for Nvidia stock.
From 2027, Nvidia is expected to devote much of its capacity at TSMC to Rubin, its next data center platform.
On its own business, Nvidia expects about 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028 and says supply is the bottleneck.
Chinese firms are leaning more on domestic suppliers like Huawei, and Nvidia also expects its gross margin to dip to 71% to 72% in Q4.
Investors in Nvidia stock should watch whether Nvidia can raise output. Any change in US export rules could also move Nvidia stock.

DETROIT — General Motors narrowed its 2026 earnings guidance and raised its free cash flow expectations after beating Wall Street's third-quarter expectations.
The Detroit automaker also announced a new multiyear stock buyback of $20 billion after GM completed a $6 billion share repurchase program that was announced in January. GM did not disclose a specific time to complete the program.
Despite the positive news, GM stock was off roughly 7% during trading Tuesday as the company's outlook missed Wall Street's expectations.
Wall Street analysts were mixed before the report on whether GM would raise its guidance Tuesday amid concerns of slowing sales and rising commodity costs. Analysts' expectations included a midpoint of $13.41 per share for the year compared with GM's new $13.25 per share midpoint, according to LSEG.
Several analysts in investor notes Tuesday said GM's third-quarter results were solid, but raised concerns about whether higher costs and pressures on vehicle pricing would limit earnings growth next year.
Here's how GM performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:
GM's new guidance includes adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $14.5 billion and $15.5 billion, or $12.75 to $13.75 adjusted earnings per share, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of between $11.5 billion and $12.5 billion.
That compares with its raised guidance from July that included adjusted EBIT of between $14 billion and $16 billion, or $12 to $14 adjusted EPS, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of $9.5 billion to $11.5 billion.
"I think the market's been pretty consistent from what we've said all year," GM CFO Paul Jacobson told CNBC's Phil LeBeau . "Our fourth quarter's going to be down sequentially. ... I think the fact that we're able to hold our guidance in the face of that late inflationary pressure in the year is another sign of the GM team executing really well."
GM on Tuesday said it expects commodity inflation costs to be around $2 billion, which was the high end of its previous guidance. That includes higher costs for logistics and dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, chips that are impacting multiple industries .
While the inflationary costs were at the automaker's high end of guidance, GM said its gross tariff costs are expected to be at the low end of its expected $2.5 billion to $3.5 billion range. Warranty costs are expected to be at high end between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, GM said.
Jacobson said vehicle pricing is relatively flat as inflationary costs continue to increase. He said the company would assess where consumers are in the coming year when deciding if it should pass costs along by raising prices more than normal.
"GM is performing well, and we are working hard to continue our momentum despite growing inflationary pressures through strategic investments in new products and services, and through improved quality and operating efficiency," GM CEO Mary Barra said Tuesday in a letter to shareholders.
The automaker also said the costs of its pullback in all-electric vehicles announced last year were "substantially completed," saying it has recorded $11.2 billion in such charges since the second half of last year, including paying $4.6 billion of $7.4 billion in cash through the third quarter.
The company's net income attributed to stockholders was $3.3 billion during the third quarter, up roughly $2 billion from a year earlier.
GM's North American operations continued to lead the automaker's results, accounting for $3.6 billion of its $4.1 billion in adjusted EBIT results during the third quarter.
GM's 2025 third-quarter results included $48.59 billion in revenue, net income attributable to stockholders of $1.3 billion and earnings per share of $2.80 adjusted.

articles.title_zh: AMD and Microsoft announce FSR 4.1 support for Xbox Series X|S and Xbox Ally, bringing huge performance gains
articles.content_orig:
