Surprise! Hot on the heels of PlayStation's own upscaling tech announcements, Microsoft and AMD just revealed that the firm's flagship FSR 4.1 tech is coming to the Xbox platform.
FSR (FidelityFX Super Resolution) is a technology from AMD that renders games at a lower resolution, and then uses machine learning to generate a sharper image. Since the hardware isn't working as hard, that overhead can be used for performance.
FSR 4.1 is a big leap over previous versions, and Microsoft has partnered with AMD to bring it not only to Xbox Series X , but also Xbox Ally X , Xbox Ally S and Xbox Series S — the latter two of which should benefit from very, very big performance boosts as a result.
"At Xbox, we're building a gaming platform designed to meet players where they are, and make it easier for creators to reach them," Xbox CTO Scott Van Vilet explained. "AMD has been an important partner in that journey for more than two decades. Together our teams have been pushing gaming forward, across Xbox and Windows. From the silicon at the heart of our consoles and handhelds, to technologies like DirectX, Advanced Shader Delivery, and AutoSR that helps developers get more from the hardware and deliver better experiences for our players."
"Today, we're excited to take another step forward together. With FSR 4.1 coming to Xbox. Now, we've worked very closely with AMD to optimize this technology, giving developers another powerful tool for great performance and visual quality for players. Now, whether you're playing on an Xbox Ally handheld, as well as coming soon to Xbox Series X and Series S consoles. And this is just the beginning. Our teams are continuing to work together across hardware and software, and there's even more ahead with Project Helix, leveraging FSR Diamond to power what comes next."
It's unclear exactly when these technologies will roll out to Xbox devices. It sounds as though FSR 4.1 will hit Xbox Ally X before the year end, but Xbox Series X|S are listed as "coming soon," with no exact window offered.
Sadly, it seems the Xbox Ally base model is fully incompatible with FSR 4.1, which is a bit of a shame, but it should prove transformative for those with the Xbox Ally X and the just-released Xbox Ally X20 , as well as the Xbox Series S.
UPDATE: I stand corrected, I just confirmed that it is also coming to the Xbox Ally base model as well!
The Xbox Series S has historically been difficult for developers owing to its irregular RAM allocation, but if FSR 4.1 can do some of the heavy lifting, it should ease the pressure on developers to deliver a native 1080p image.
We're reaching out to Microsoft for some clarification on timelines and will get back to you if we hear from them.

articles.title_orig: UK to send jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: UK to send jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
The United Kingdom said Tuesday it will deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by the Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen.
The UK will fly “defensive counter-air missions” using Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
Over the past month, the Houthis have intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia, launching ballistic missiles and drones at key infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports.
The UK is already providing air-to-air refueling support to Saudi Arabia and has deployed air defense equipment and British personnel to help protect the kingdom, a spokesperson for the prime minister’s office told reporters.
The Typhoons will intercept missiles and drones launched against Saudi Arabia and will not conduct offensive strikes inside Yemen, the spokesperson said.
The conflict has been intensifying since the Houthis announced in July that they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea as well as infrastructure inside the kingdom, following a Saudi attack on the Houthi-controlled airport in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa.
They have stepped up their attacks in recent weeks, launching repeated strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport. One such strike killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, making it the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
Saudi Arabia has looked for military support from regional and Western allies to counter the intensified Houthi attacks. France agreed to deploy defense assets, including military personnel, and more than 100 American military advisers are on the ground providing intelligence and targeting support under a newly established joint forces command.
Pakistan has forces stationed in Saudi Arabia, and the Egyptian parliament is debating whether to send support after President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called an emergency session to deploy military assistance to the kingdom.
“The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable,” UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said in a statement. “The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region.”
Last month, the Iran-allied rebel group launched a lightning offensive on Yemen’s western coast, capturing key territory. That included the Bab al-Mandeb maritime chokepoint on the Red Sea, potentially expanding Tehran’s influence over another trade corridor.
Saudi Arabia cancels next week’s ‘Davos in the Desert’ conference after series of Houthi attacks
Backed by Saudi warplanes, Yemen’s anti-Houthi government ground forces have launched a counteroffensive to recapture lost territory. Despite a heavy airstrike campaign and a large ground offensive, Houthi rebels have retained control over key locations and have continued launching missiles and drones at their adversaries.
At least 53 newly recruited Yemeni government forces were killed by the Houthis in a ballistic missile attack Monday on the southeastern Shabwa province, local officials said. More than 200 others were reported wounded.
The attack was condemned by the US mission to Yemen, which called it a “cowardly attack by the Iran-backed Houthi militia” on Yemenis who had “volunteered to keep their communities and country safe.”
This story has been updated with additional developments.
James Frater contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Trump Tariffs on Canada Spark Latest Lawsuit Over Trade Powers
articles.title_zh: Trump Tariffs on Canada Spark Latest Lawsuit Over Trade Powers
articles.content_orig:
A new lawsuit filed Tuesday challenges President Donald Trump 's invocation of a Depression-era law to impose 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods .
Trump in July used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap those steep tariffs on Canadian hockey sticks, wine, honey, wigs, and other products in response to alleged trade discrimination by Ottawa. It was the first time the 96-year-old law had ever been used to impose a tariff.
"Section 338 is a relic of the retaliation-based tariff policy" that has been "impliedly repealed" by subsequent legislation, the civil complaint filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade says.
The suit was filed by Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based food importer that says its cheeses are covered by the tariffs. The complaint asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful, block their enforcement, and order the Trump administration to issue refunds for duties already paid, with interest.
Gellert Global is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the same legal group that dealt a major blow to Trump's trade agenda by successfully contesting his "reciprocal" tariffs.
The Supreme Court struck those tariffs down in February. The administration is in the process of refunding the estimated $166 billion that the federal government collected from importers through the reciprocal duties.
The Liberty Justice Center is currently engaged in two other lawsuits against what it says is Trump's misuse of laws to impose sweeping tariffs.
"This case is not about the president. It is about the presidency," the group's CEO Sara Albrecht said in a statement Tuesday morning announcing Gellert Global's suit. "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required."
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the suit.

articles.title_orig: Yemen’s Taiz faces deadly siege, as Shabwah death toll rises
articles.title_zh: Yemen’s Taiz faces deadly siege, as Shabwah death toll rises
articles.content_orig:
The siege on Taiz has cut humanitarian supplies to the Yemeni city, the United Nations has warned, and left many of its inhabitants without food and other essentials.
UN Human Rights Chief Volker Turk said on Tuesday that the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), who have surrounded the city, must immediately allow humanitarian relief to enter or risk a catastrophe.
“The Houthis’ closure of the only supply route linking Taiz to Aden is placing civilians at grave risk, blocking humanitarian aid and cutting off essential supplies,” the high commissioner said.
“Humanitarian aid must be immediately allowed to enter the city and its passage must be facilitated. Civilians wishing to leave must be allowed to do so freely and safely.”
Taiz, which has been repeatedly besieged throughout the war, has been encircled again by the Houthis after they captured a major road linking the city to southern Yemen.
The humanitarian situation in Taiz is reaching a breaking point with the prices of basic commodities multiplying in price, amid shortages of some goods.
Continued fighting in Taiz governorate has also killed at least 32 civilians between August 1 and October 19, including 14 children. There are fears of more deaths as fighting approaches the city.
“I urge all parties to the conflict to refrain from the use of explosive weapons with wide-area effects in populated areas and to take all feasible precautions to protect civilians and civilian objects,” Turk said.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government had appealed to the United Nations to intervene and lift the blockade, warning that the Houthi siege threatens more than 4 million people.
The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that shifting front lines and road closures have cut off 800,000 people from life-saving assistance, the vast majority located in Taiz. Nationwide, more than 18 million Yemenis face severe food insecurity.
Forces aligned with the internationally-recognised government on Monday launched air strikes in Taiz governorate that destroyed Houthi reinforcements in Najd Qasim and a weapons depot in Jabal Habashi.
The Yemeni government added on Tuesday that its forces had stopped Houthi attempts to advance across Taiz, incuding in al-Shaqab, al-Misrakh, al-Aqroudh, and Jabal Han.
On Tuesday, local authorities raised the death toll from a Houthi attack on a military base in Shabwa governorate to 73.
Monday’s Houthi ballistic missile strikes on al-Alam camp were condemned by the Yemeni government as a “treacherous bloody assault” and a war crime.
President of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council Rashad al-Alimi formally requested the UN to designate the Houthis as a “terrorist organisation”.
The United Kingdom said on Tuesday it would deploy fighter jets to help protect Saudi Arabia from attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, after cities and infrastructure were targeted in rocket and drone attacks.
The British Ministry of Defence said that Typhoon warplanes would play a “defensive role” only and would not carry out attacks in Yemen.
Egypt’s parliament meanwhile delayed a vote on Monday to authorise the military to support Saudi Arabia in its fight against the Houthis.
Ali al-Dahab, a military and security strategic affairs expert, said that while there appears to be more international support for the anti-Houthi alliance, this will not likely translate into boots on the ground in Yemen.
“The probability of international ground forces engaging to confront the Houthis seems slim; expected participation will be limited to air and naval support,” he told Al Jazeera.
The Yemeni military launched a sweeping offensive dubbed “Dawn of Yemen” on 5 October to reverse recent Houthi advances. But despite initial successes in the early days of the campaign, with hundreds of Houthi fighters reportedly killed in air strikes, there are questions about whether these counter-offensives have run out of steam.
“The transition from defence to offence remains limited on the ground, and the map of the Yemeni government’s influence in al-Marib [an energy-rich part of central Yemen] has not expanded to the extent implied by the meaning of the [operation],” al-Dahab told Al Jazeera.
“Government forces must exploit the gaps created by conventional and drone air strikes in Houthi ranks by launching a multi-directional operation that turns this into a strategic shift, specifically in the northwestern direction toward Sanaa.”
The intensification of ground battles in Yemen has triggered a wave of cross-border attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi-led coalition said Tuesday it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh. The attack prompted the Saudi Civil Defense to activate early warning platforms across the capital.
The Arab coalition has launched waves of strikes on Houthi positions across Yemen during the past week.
“On the strategic and long-term, [aerial attrition strikes] can have a tangible impact on the Houthis’ military infrastructure, structures, machines, and vehicles,” al-Dahab said.
However, he questioned the government’s ability to capitalise on these strikes on the western coast, where the Yemeni government is attempting to claw back losses from the Houthis.
“Do government forces have enough power to launch an attack toward Mocha on the coast or toward Hodeidah?” al-Dahab asked, noting that Houthi fighters are desperately holding onto the Kahboub mountains in Lahij for their commanding maritime view over the Gulf of Aden and the southern Red Sea.

articles.title_orig: Here's how to preorder Apple's HomeView smart display — plus alternatives to shop now
articles.title_zh: Here's how to preorder Apple's HomeView smart display — plus alternatives to shop now
articles.content_orig:
Apple’s new HomeView was reportedly mostly finished for years, but kept getting delayed. Here’s why HomeView couldn’t launch until now, per quotes from key Apple execs.
In November 2024, Mark Gurman published an in-depth report on the product we now know as HomeView. At the time, he said Apple was targeting a March 2025 launch. But that date kept slipping, and now HomeView will finally arrive in homes on November 13, 2026.
Why the long wait? Gurman has repeatedly pointed to Siri AI as the chief cause of delays. And Apple execs have now largely confirmed that in quotes given to The Verge .
Jennifer Pattison Tuohy asked Kaiann Drance, Apple’s VP of product marketing for home, why now was the right time for HomeView and Apple’s renewed smart home push.
She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said.
HomeView is being marketed as a shared device that taps into users’ personal context in a way that wasn’t possible pre-Siri AI. So it’s easy to see how Apple’s main pitch would need to change without the more personalized Siri.
A similar explanation was given by Apple’s Lilian Rincon, VP of product marketing for AI. She told The Verge that Siri AI is core to HomeView because it’s “much more capable” and also highlighted its conversational abilities, which make it easy to use for any family member.
“It’s great because you can just ask it to change the temperature on your thermostat in a very natural way. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.”
This device is extremely redundant. I’m sure mostly everyone almost always has their phone on their person, to where this device isn’t needed. iPhone, iPad, and Apple TV can do all the things that HomeView can offer.
This emphasis and explanation also makes HomeView’s absence in the EU more understandable.
If Siri AI was simply a nice-to-have addition to an otherwise feature-rich product, perhaps it could launch in the EU still. But if the whole value proposition revolves around the new assistant and its personalized features, waiting until Siri AI is available for iOS in the EU makes more sense.
You can read The Verge’s full article here for more quotes and context.

articles.title_orig: Over 1.5M pounds of meat recalled over serious potential health concerns
articles.title_zh: Over 1.5M pounds of meat recalled over serious potential health concerns
articles.content_orig:
The USDA on Saturday announced a recall on dozens of pork, beef, and chicken products from Chelsea-based Kayem Foods Inc., the brand known for its Fenway Franks.
The more than 1.5 million pounds of hot dogs, sausages, bacon, and other products have been voluntarily recalled after the company learned the goods had been stored in a cooler that experienced “temperature deviation,” Kayem said in a statement on Friday .
“Our business depends on providing consumers with safe food of the highest quality,” said Matt Monkiewicz, Kayem Foods president and CEO. “Out of an abundance of caution, we are undertaking this voluntary recall.”
The meat items were distributed from the company’s Chelsea warehouse to stores and food service locations across the US and in Hong Kong, according to the US Department of Agriculture .
There have been no confirmed reports of illness due to consumption of the products, and anyone concerned about an illness should contact a doctor, the USDA statement said.
Many of the products recalled are hot dogs and hams that can be stored for long periods in the freezer. All the items affected by the recall were shipped between June 7, 2026, and Oct. 14, 2026, the company statement said.
The USDA said its Food Safety and Inspection Service team was concerned consumers may have recalled products in their refrigerators.
“Consumers who have purchased these products are urged not to consume them. These products should be thrown away or returned to the place of purchase,” the USDA said.
Other recalled products include chicken sausage, bologna, beef brisket, corned beef, and liverwurst, according to documents published by the USDA and Kayem that showed dozens of item labels.
The problem was discovered after Kayem received a complaint from a retail store about warm product temperatures “at point of delivery” on Oct. 1, the USDA said.
Kayem investigated and determined they had stored various meat and poultry products in a warehouse cooler that experienced temperature deviations, said spokesperson Kraig Naasz.
The problem with the warehouse cooler was caused by “a cooling system malfunction,” Kayem said in its news release Friday.
“We take food safety very seriously and apologize to our valued consumers. Our management team takes full responsibility. We have learned from and corrected the issue and will not allow this to happen again,” said Monkiewicz in the statement.
The company also said it is contacting each of its wholesale and retail customers directly with instructions to identify and dispose of the recalled products.
A full list of recalled items with images of package labeling and how to identify affected products can be found on Kayem’s website .

articles.title_orig: Chip stocks recover as AI jitters fade
articles.title_zh: Chip stocks recover as AI jitters fade
articles.content_orig:
It was a bumpy week in the markets, with semiconductor stocks selling off sharply as worries about the durability of the artificial intelligence trade weighed on sentiment. Meanwhile, shares of CoreWeave CRWV plunged when its debt accrued to fund data center construction began trading at levels indicating distress.
Data center bonds also scraped fresh lows last week, as Cipher Digital’s new debt raise fueled investor anxieties on AI overspending. CoreWeave bonds bore the brunt of the selloff.
In this week’s Market Brief:
As semiconductor names plunged, investors backed out of growth stocks and value climbed higher, with the Morningstar US Core Cap Growth Index down 1.9% for the week through Thursday, while the Morningstar US Core Cap Value Index was up 0.6%.
The Morningstar Global Semiconductors Index tumbled 5.8% through Thursday’s close, with Nvidia NVDA down 5.2%, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing TSM down 8.4%, and Broadcom AVGO down 7.8%.
In fixed income, bonds fell as investors sought safety outside of equities. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note dropped to 5.13% after peaking at 5.32% earlier in the week.
Even as the AI trade remains volatile, some strategists are still constructive on the sector. In emailed commentary on Thursday, Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and global head of equities at the UBS Chief Investment Office, wrote: “While increased competition within AI, rising financing requirements, and higher rates may periodically add to volatility, we view this latest bout as more of a recalibration of expectations than a fundamental break in the AI investment story. We suggest investors focus on where AI spending is translating into sustainable earnings growth and broader enterprise and consumer adoption.”
Is AI really driving up inflation? From Wall Street to the Federal Reserve and beyond, the buildout of AI infrastructure is often cited as a major source of upward pressure on prices. In new research released this week, Goldman Sachs economists argue that AI’s effect on prices is both overstated and near its peak. They looked under the hood of the AI buildout, considering its impact on software prices, its effect on the price of computer components, the demand for power from data centers and the associated increase in electricity prices, and the rising prices of the industrial metals used in the construction of data centers.
Overall, the economists found that AI is responsible for a roughly 0.45% increase in CPE inflation, and that half that figure is attributable to the actual impact of AI rather than measurement errors. They describe that impact as “meaningful but moderate,” and expect that it is near its peak, which they forecast as a 0.5% boost by the end of 2026. By the end of 2027, they expect only a 0.1% boost to PCE inflation from AI as memory and computer price growth slows.
“Even if we took all of the AI impact at face value and assumed instead that it would persist next year, we would still expect core PCE inflation to fall meaningfully toward the 2% target,” they write, pointing to the fading impact of tariffs and the Iran war energy shock.
For more on AI and inflation, read Morningstar chief US economist Preston Caldwell’s take .
Big Tech stocks carried the market to record highs in recent weeks. Now, their earnings may determine whether the rally continues. Investors will watch two key metrics in hyperscaler earnings reports coming over the next few weeks, according to Morningstar equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan.
The first is cloud growth at Microsoft MSFT , Alphabet GOOG / GOOGL , and Amazon AMZN . Last quarter, all three reported accelerating cloud revenue growth, and investors are hoping for a repeat. Microsoft forecast its Azure revenue growth would accelerate to 45% from 42% in the prior quarter. Neither Alphabet nor Amazon provided cloud growth forecasts, but Khan expects their revenue will get a boost from custom chip sales.
The second metric is capital expenditures. The hyperscalers are on track to spend more than $750 billion on capex this year, about double their 2025 spending. Khan expects the hyperscalers to provide “directional commentary on next year’s capex,” giving markets an idea of the trajectory of AI spending.
Whether cloud growth and capex meet expectations could have a massive impact on the stock market broadly. Investors are nervous about whether AI investments will pay off. They worry that hyperscalers will overbuild, causing compute prices to plummet and saddling the cloud giants with unused capacity. They also fear that frontier labs OpenAI and Anthropic won’t have the cash to make good on their spending commitments, which account for a large chunk of hyperscaler backlogs. For those reasons, “the market is pretty negative [on capex],” says Khan.
However, hyperscalers could justify high capex by proving that they’re seeing a return on investment. For Meta, that could mean showing that users are regularly engaging and making transactions with its Muse AI agents. For the other hyperscalers, cloud growth is the clearest evidence of ROI.
If hyperscalers can’t convince investors their AI spending is wise, other stocks will suffer. “The overall AI trade could materially be thrown off if these cloud businesses don’t actually show returns,” says Khan. Chip, power, and certain software stocks would all be at risk. “Everything that has run up because of AI, all of that is counting on demand being real.”

articles.title_orig: You Should Probably Check Your Google Home Speaker’s Data Usage
articles.title_zh: You Should Probably Check Your Google Home Speaker’s Data Usage
articles.content_orig:
The new Google Home Speaker has an issue where it downloads hundreds of gigabytes of data in the background for some owners.
Over the past week, several reports have emerged about how the Google Home Speaker appears to be continuously downloading data from company servers.
In my case, a Google Home Speaker that has not been used in the past day for voice commands or media streaming consumed 17 GB of data in 24 hours. At 3 a.m. PT, it downloaded 9.99 GB. Given the timing, this could be related to failed attempts to download device firmware.
Meanwhile, on October 13, the same speaker downloaded 41 GB of data. Over the past 30 days, the total download comes in at 132 GB.
It’s not clear if this is a widespread issue. Another lightly used Home Speaker of ours (in a different household) downloaded only 2 GB of data in the past month.
That doesn't make sense how much storage does it have? It's just downloading and deleting constantly?
Most routers let you check how much data a particular device has used. If you’re using Nest Wifi, go to the Google Home app’s Wifi top tab > Devices > select your speaker > Device usage graphs. You can switch between 1-, 7-, and 30-day graphs.
We’re not seeing this download issue with other Google Home and Nest devices, including several Nest Hubs in the same house as the affected Home Speaker.
If you have multiple Home Speakers and a limited data plan, this issue could easily breach your cap, as some have found.
In a statement to 9to5Google today, the company acknowledged the issue and said “a fix is already rolling out that should address this for users.”

articles.title_orig: Global oil prices hit highest level in 5 months amid attacks on ships, facilities - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Global oil prices hit highest level in 5 months amid attacks on ships, facilities - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Global oil prices have climbed more than 55% since the outbreak of the Iran war.
Global oil prices climbed to their highest level in five months on Tuesday after Iran and its Houthi allies claimed attacks on oil infrastructure in the Middle East.
The Brent crude futures price, a benchmark for global trading, topped $111 a barrel for the first time since May before retreating to $110.30 a barrel. The latest reading marks a rise of more than 55% since the Iran war began in late February.
An oil shortage continues to bedevil crude sellers, who typically pass along elevated costs to refiners, leading to higher prices at the pump.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center, or UKMTO, on Tuesday issued an advisory after it received a report of an incident involving a tanker and military forces off the coast of Oman.
Separately, Iranian state-run media reported on Tuesday that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed that two oil tankers hit naval mines south of the Strait of Hormuz.
The reports came a day after Yemen-based Houthi militants claimed a wave of strikes on Saudia Arabia on Monday, including the Shaybah oil field as well as Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a port city near a key transport corridor on the Red Sea.
The West Texas Intermediate futures price, a benchmark index for U.S. trading, also jumped on Tuesday. The price of U.S. oil prices stands at $105.75, a rise of more than 60% since the outbreak of the war.
The jump in oil prices arrived as affordability marks a top concern for voters ahead of early November's midterm elections .
The average price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. clocked in at $4.27 on Tuesday, according to AAA . That figure amounts to a rise of nearly $1.30 since the start late February.
The Middle East conflict drove up fuel prices and catapulted U.S. inflation to a three-year high in May, but inflation eased slightly over the summer after a preliminary peace agreement established an on-again, off-again pause in fighting.
The tentative accord between the U.S. and Iran expired in August, giving way to continued attacks on oil infrastructure and ships in the region.
The U.S. -- the world's largest oil producer -- imports a small amount of crude from the Middle East. Since oil and gas are sold on a global market, however, the shortage has sent prices rising for everyone, including U.S. drivers.
ABC News' Nasser Atta, Othon Leyva and Desiree Adib contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq mixed as AI trade rebound stalls
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks climbed on Tuesday as chip stocks trimmed losses and investors turned their focus to a slew of earnings out this week.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 0.9%, and the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) gained 0.4%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) erased its decline, climbing 0.2% after the major averages closed mixed on Monday, as tech stocks rebounded.
The AI trade came into focus on Tuesday after Elice ( 0158S0.KQ ), a South Korean data center provider, saw its shares plunge 32% during its public debut in Seoul, underscoring lingering concerns about the health of the AI trade.
Investors turned their attention to a fresh round of corporate earnings this week. General Motors ( GM ) tightened its profit outlook but announced a $20 billion share buyback program . United Airlines ( UAL ) will report after the close.
Streaming giant Netflix ( NFLX ) will report quarterly earnings after the bell on Tuesday. EV maker Tesla ( TSLA ) and social media giant Meta ( META ) are expected to post results on Wednesday.
On the economic front, housing starts fell to a four-month low amid soft demand, with mortgage rates remaining elevated.
Brent crude futures ( BZ=F ) fell to $108 per barrel while West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) traded below $98.
Qualcomm ( QCOM ) shares rose 1% following a report that the designer of chips for smartphones plans to start cutting jobs globally next month as part of a "performance-focused reduction" following employee reviews.
The plan was outlined in a memo to staff from CEO Cristiano Amon, which Reuters reviewed. Notifications are set to start in November.
The memo did not specify how many positions would be affected.
Qualcomm shares are up more than 2% year-to-date.
Wall Street is in a buying mood. The AI trade's leaders had to bleed a little before joining in.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) slipped below Friday's close early, giving back Monday's rebound from an eight-session losing streak, as my colleague Ines Ferré reported . Then buyers showed up right at the summer floor near 11,000.
Chart watchers know this setup.
A dip below support that quickly reverses is a bear trap , catching traders who bet on a breakdown. But it only counts if chips close back above Friday's level.
And history says don't relax yet. After every losing streak of seven sessions or more since 1994, the index traded below the streak's final close within a month. After the longest ones, it was lower a month later most of the time.
A BofA Global Research report calls last week's rout a "positioning-driven hiccup on the fringes of the AI trade." The credit market isn't so sure. The cost of insuring Oracle's debt is at its highest since at least 2021, and even the megacaps' default swaps are creeping up.
A close above 11,137 springs the trap. Lose 11,000, and the next stop is closer to 10,450.
US stocks were mixed at Tuesday's open as investors weighed another batch of corporate earnings against pressure from higher government bond yields.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 0.4% while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell 0.1%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) declined 0.5% after the major averages closed mixed on Monday as tech stocks rebounded.
Investors remain focused on whether strong third-quarter earnings can keep stocks moving higher after last week's volatility. At Tuesday's open the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ) hovered at 5.10%, keeping pressure on stock valuations though easing over the last week.
AI infrastructure stocks are under pressure again before the opening bell. CoreWeave ( CRWV ) is taking the hardest hit.
The AI cloud provider is trading at its lowest level since May 2025 premarket, extending a slide of more than 40% since Oct. 6.
So what's spooking investors? The debt. CoreWeave borrowed heavily to build its data centers, and its bonds sold off across maturities last week, as my colleague Brian Sozzi reported .
Siebert Financial chief investment officer Mark Malek isn't rushing in. Some AI stocks are "honestly down for the right reason," he said Monday on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang. He "wouldn't back up the truck."
Every chip stock trading premarket in a 60-stock Yahoo Finance semiconductor basket is lower, with SK hynix ( SKHY ) and Nebius ( NBIS ) among the hardest hit. The rest of the market is calmer, with S&P 500 gainers outnumbering decliners roughly 3 to 2.
Monday's low of $59.25 is the line in the sand. A snap back above it would make this breakdown a bear trap — a fake-out that burns traders betting on more losses.
Stay below, and the next stops are around $53, then the all-time low at $33 and change.
Yahoo Finance's Pras Subramanian reports:
GM ( GM ) posted third quarter results before the bell that topped estimates. The automaker tightened its full-year profit outlook instead of boosting it, but issued shareholders a new $20 billion share repurchase program instead.
For the quarter, GM posted Q3 revenue of $50.0 billion, up 2.9% from a year ago and above the $48.52 billion Bloomberg consensus. GM posted adjusted EPS of $3.70 vs $3.57 estimated, with adjusted EBIT coming in at $4.1 billion, ahead of the $4.02 billion expected and up nearly 22%.
President Trump announced an $8 billion aid package on Monday to help US farmers pay for diesel this harvest season.
The relief program, announced at a campaign rally in Kansas and on social media, aims to bring down fuel costs for Americans ahead of next month's midterm elections.
"Tonight, I am also pleased to announce that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new 'Harvest Fuel Relief Program,' providing our Farmers with 8 BILLION DOLLARS in support to offset Diesel costs during this Harvest Season," Trump's account posted on Truth Social ( DJT ).

articles.title_orig: Kaja Kallas accuses the US of pushing Ukraine to 'surrender on Putin's terms'
articles.title_zh: Kaja Kallas accuses the US of pushing Ukraine to 'surrender on Putin's terms'
articles.content_orig:
The European Union must step up its efforts in three areas in response to Russian attacks in the Black Sea: ensure Ukrainian agricultural exports, strengthen maritime security, and increase international diplomatic pressure on Russia.
Kallas outlined three areas of a joint European response to the escalation of Russian attacks, which threaten Ukrainian export routes and global food security.
“Russia’s actions are making it harder to feed people around the world. And this requires a strong and united European response along three lines,” Kallas stated.
The first area is preserving Ukraine’s access to global markets and safeguarding global food security.
According to Kallas, the EU is working to ensure that Ukraine remains connected to global markets and that its agricultural exports have alternative routes.
“We are working to ensure that Ukraine remains connected to global markets and to safeguard food security. The EU-Ukraine ‘Solidarity Lanes’ initiative is helping to identify alternative routes, and since July, grain exports via the ‘Solidarity Lanes’ have increased by nearly 2 million metric tons,” Kallas said.
At the same time, Russia has begun attacking border crossings with Moldova, Romania, and Poland , threatening alternative export routes for Ukrainian products.
Kallas also reported that due to intensified Russian attacks on export routes , Ukraine has been losing 60 million euros in export revenue every day since mid-July .
The second priority is strengthening security in the Black Sea and on the Danube. To achieve this, Kallas emphasized, it is necessary to improve information sharing and promptly identify potential threats.
“Early detection and real-time information sharing are of key importance,” the EU High Representative stressed.
According to her, thanks to the MARSUR network, EU member states can exchange maritime surveillance data and improve their shared situational awareness at sea.
In addition, Romania and Bulgaria, with EU support , are establishing the Black Sea Maritime Security Center . It is intended to help European countries better monitor the situation in the region.
Kallas also stressed the need to develop capabilities to counter air and maritime threats. In this regard, the EU is promoting the joint development of defense capabilities and procurement, particularly within the framework of the drone coalition.
Another tool will be the Eastern Flank Watch initiative, designed to strengthen surveillance and defense on Europe’s eastern flank—from the Baltic to the Black Sea—in close coordination with NATO.
At the same time, through the European Defense Agency, EU countries are already collaborating on the development of next-generation maritime mine countermeasures and unmanned maritime systems .
The third area of focus is increasing international diplomatic pressure on Russia and ensuring freedom of navigation in the Black Sea.
Kallas recalled that on September 23 in New York , 51 countries and the European Union issued a joint statement condemning Russian aggression and calling for freedom of navigation in the Black Sea.
The European Union continues to work with international partners to reach relevant agreements.
“We are currently working with international partners—Turkey, India, and others, including African countries for which food is of vital importance, and more broadly—with countries of the Global South—to secure an agreement on freedom of navigation in the Black Sea,” the EU’s top diplomat said.
Thus, the European response to Russian attacks involves supporting Ukrainian exports, strengthening maritime surveillance and defense capabilities, and expanding the international coalition to protect freedom of navigation .
This was stated by the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Kaja Kallas, during a plenary debate in the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Tuesday, October 20.
In the Black Sea near Bulgaria and Romania, six merchant ships were attacked by drones over a 10-day period. At least 11 sailors were killed in the attacks, and crew members from several ships remain missing.
In October, drones attacked at least seven cargo ships in the Black Sea near Romania and Bulgaria. Two people were killed in these incidents, and at least 25 others are considered missing. The attacks took place in the exclusive economic zones of two NATO countries and pose a threat to a vital international shipping route.

Homebuyers are backing out of contracts at near-record rates, a potential sign of how higher mortgage rates are prompting buyers to rethink their plans.
Nationwide, 14.5% of homes fell out of contract in September, according to Redfin data, the highest share on record apart from the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Read more: Why the housing market is in for 'a challenging couple months'
Homes can fall out of contract for a number of reasons, such as inspection findings or financing pitfalls, or when a buyer just has a change of heart. But pending sales tend to fall through at higher rates when buyers have more options and more negotiating power, as they currently do in much of the country.
Indeed, metro areas that are notably buyer's markets, like Jacksonville and Tampa, Fla., and Las Vegas, all had contract cancellation rates approaching 20%, higher than anywhere else in the country. But they're relatively rare in strong seller's markets like San Francisco, where just 2.8% of deals fell apart.

articles.title_orig: FedEx truck robbed of trading cards worth over $963,000 outside PSA headquarters - The Athletic
articles.title_zh: FedEx truck robbed of trading cards worth over $963,000 outside PSA headquarters - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
Thieves carried out a high-stakes heist outside the Santa Ana headquarters of a trading card authenticator, stealing nearly $1 million worth of collectibles from a parked FedEx truck.
Authorities said the truck was unattended outside the home base of grading giant Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) on Oct. 13, when opportunistic crooks swiped nearly 250 packages — two pallets carrying an estimated 100 packages each, and a third holding 50 more.
“The pallets contained various trading cards, including, but not limited to, sports cards and Pokémon cards,” the Santa Ana Police Department told the California Post.
Police said the driver left the vehicle unattended outside PSA’s headquarters for 60 to 90 minutes. Authorities said the truck’s lock was broken and the packages were stolen while the driver was away.
“The estimated value of the stolen cards at the time of the incident was $963,000. However, the exact value of the stolen items has not yet been determined,” the SAPD said.
PSA parent company Collectors said that certificates used to identify each individual card were deactivated for all the stolen items and trading partners were notified so that they can be on the lookout for rare and serialized cards.
“We are aware of a theft involving a third-party shipping vehicle carrying PSA-graded items. We are working closely with law enforcement and the carrier as the investigation continues,” Collectors’ statement read.
Famous card collector and YouTuber Sky-B Cards claims to have shelled out an $8,468 in grading fees alone for a prized 104-card order, which was insured for up to $156,000.
“These were 104 cards that I’ve accumulated over two years. There are many irreplaceable cards in here that I will never see again,” Sky-B said in a video update .
There have been no arrests so far and the investigation remains ongoing. SAPD urges anyone with information regarding this incident to contact the department.

A judge has dismissed a civil lawsuit filed by Sam Altman’s sister accusing the OpenAI co-founder and chief executive of repeated sexual abuse more than two decades ago, an accusation he denies.
In dismissing Annie Altman's lawsuit , US District Judge Zachary Bluestone wrote that she refused to appear for an independent medical examination despite warnings that failing to do so would result in the case's dismissal.
Laura Politi, a lawyer for Annie Altman, did not immediately comment on the dismissal. Santos Perez, a lawyer who previously represented Annie Altman in the case but withdrew this month, said in a statement, "I am no longer authorized to comment on this case but I continue to believe in Annie."
Lawyers for Sam Altman, who became a face of the artificial intelligence boom after the chatbot ChatGPT was released in 2022, did not immediately comment.
Annie Altman brought her lawsuit in St. Louis, Missouri, federal court in January 2025.
She accused her brother of sexually abusing and raping her between 1997 and 2006 at the family home in suburban Clayton, Missouri, starting when she was 3 and he was 12. She said the last acts of sexual abuse and rape occurred when Sam Altman was an adult. He is now 41.
The Altman family has said Annie Altman has mental health challenges and received financial support. Sam Altman has said she began accusing him on social media of sexual abuse after the family rejected her demands for more funds.
If you are a child and you need help because something has happened to you, you can call Childline free of charge on 0800 1111. You can also call the NSPCC if you are an adult and you are worried about a child, on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adults on 0808 801 0331

articles.title_orig: Australian MP hit by vehicle has leg amputated - as suspect's father says she is family friend
articles.title_zh: Australian MP hit by vehicle has leg amputated - as suspect's father says she is family friend
articles.content_orig:
A 43-year-old man has been charged after Australian MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in the state of Victoria on Monday.
The suspect will appear in court on Wednesday to face charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official.
Local media earlier named the alleged attacker as environmental activist Brendan Nugent. His father and his partner said they had been friends with Haines "for more than 20 years" and thanked residents and officers who helped her after the "shocking and horrific crime".
Haines remains in a critical condition after surgery and is reported to have lost one of her legs.
"Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community," Rod Nugent and his partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement.
"All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends."
They promised to assist Victoria Police "in any way we can".
Police say they will allege the incident was targeted.
Haines, 65, the independent member for Indi, is in a critical but stable condition after undergoing surgery at a Melbourne hospital.
She was airlifted there after bystanders rushed to help.
A local barber who was there says he pulled the suspect out of his car.
"I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I was just a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish way," said Ricky Jefferies.
Others who helped "didn't even check for danger", he added. "The car was still on and they sat in front of a rolling car, that's not an exaggeration."
In their statement, Victoria Police say a highway patrol unit was nearby at the time of the incident and "on scene" within eight seconds of the call coming through.
As they announced the charges against the 43-year-old, they said they had searched a property in Tarrawingee, around 12km (7.5 miles) from Wangaratta.
"At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are currently no other known threats connected to this matter," they said, adding officers would maintain a presence in Wangaratta.
Haines won the seat of Indi as an independent in 2019, and has since become a prominent member of the crossbench, building rapport across Australia's increasingly divided political spectrum.
The community, and country, remain in shock.
At a vigil on Tuesday, locals queued patiently in the aisle of the Holy Trinity Cathedral, waiting for their turn to light a candle. Priests hugged some of those who came to pay their respects.
Wangaratta's main street, where Haines's office is located, had reopened to traffic. Cars slowly filed past the growing number of bouquets being left for her on the pavement.
One card read: "May you recover quickly and continue to be a light in this world."

articles.title_orig: Oil prices move higher as traders adjust to a new normal in the Middle East
articles.title_zh: Oil prices move higher as traders adjust to a new normal in the Middle East
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell Tuesday as traders hoped for diplomatic progress between the U.S. and Iran, though attacks on tankers and strikes against Saudi Arabia have escalated recently.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November were down 0.9% at $102.75 per barrel, pulling back dramatically from a session high of $110.48. The November contract expires on Tuesday. The WTI December contract was down 1% at $97.50 per barrel.
Global benchmark Brent crude futures for December delivery fell 1% to $108.31 per barrel,  well off a session high of $111.99.
Developments in the Middle East remain in focus, with attacks on commercial ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz escalating in recent weeks. At least 18 vessels have come under fire over the past two weeks, according to ship tracker Kpler.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said Tuesday that two "non-compliant" oil tankers had been set ablaze in the strait after hitting mines laid by its naval unit, Iranian state-affiliated news agency Tasnim reported.
Meanwhile, Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said at a weekly news conference on Tuesday that Tehran would respond to any American strike "in equal measure, if not more forcefully," according to Tasnim.
U.S. President Donald Trump said earlier this month that American forces will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Tamas Varga, analyst at PVM Oil Associates, told CNBC in an email on Tuesday that front-end WTI strength ahead of the contract expiry is a sign of tightness in the global crude oil market.
"It is a reflection of falling export volumes from the Middle East as tanker attacks and Houthi strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure intensify," he said. "Secondly, the U.S. decision to exempt Russian shadow fleet from sanctions will push freight rates possibly lower, which was a prohibitive factor to increase demand for U.S.-sourced crude."
"With this hurdle removed, at least temporary, U.S. crude oil grades are back in play as replacements of Mideast crude oil," he added. "Thirdly, U.S. commercial oil stocks are expected to have declined last week."

articles.title_orig: Walmart rolls out new bundle combining Walmart+, Sam’s Club Plus
articles.title_zh: Walmart rolls out new bundle combining Walmart+, Sam’s Club Plus
articles.content_orig:
Walmart on Tuesday debuted a discounted joint membership with Sam's Club, the retailer's warehouse club, in a bid to attract inflation-weary customers.
Walmart said it's offering a combined Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus membership for $120 a year, saving shoppers who buy them individually about $100 annually, according to the company.
The joint membership gives customers access to members-only discounted prices at Sam's Club, free delivery on goods from both retailers, a Peacock or Paramount+ subscription plan, 10 cents off on gas at 17,000 stations across the U.S. and rewards on eligible purchases (Paramount+ is owned by Skydance, which also owns CBS News).
"For $120 a year, we're raising expectations for what a membership can deliver: more money in their pockets and more time to call their own," Walmart CEO John Furner said in a statement.
Existing members can also upgrade their plans. Walmart+ members can switch to the dual membership for $22 more per year, while Club members can upgrade to Sam's Club Plus for $60 more per year, which includes Walmart+.
Walmart is betting that low prices and discounts will draw cash-strapped Americans into its stores. In August, Chief Financial Officer John Rainey announced price cuts across a range of products, including food.
"We're investing heavily in price because customers need us to and because we believe it drives market share gains over time," Rainey said at the time.
Walmart's efforts to ease prices come as consumers continue to grapple with elevated inflation, with the Consumer Price Index rising at an annual rate of 3.7% in September .
After five years of elevated inflation, nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their economic outlook, according to a recent CBS News poll.

articles.title_orig: UK to deploy fighter jets to help Saudis against Houthi attacks
articles.title_zh: UK to deploy fighter jets to help Saudis against Houthi attacks
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — U.K. fighter jets will be sent to aid Saudi Arabia in defending itself against attacks on critical energy and civilian infrastructure by the Houthis.
The Iranian-backed Islamist militia group, based in civil war-hit Yemen, has been launching ballistic missile strikes on Saudi Arabia for the past few weeks, successfully hitting three airports earlier this month.
The Ministry of Defence announced Tuesday that Royal Air Force Typhoon fighters will be deployed to the Gulf Kingdom — while stressing that they will be only used in a defensive capacity.
U.K. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the “continuing attacks” on the U.K.’s ally are “absolutely despicable.”
“The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region,” he added, referencing the attacks earlier this month that killed 14 people and injured hundreds more.
Streeting said that the fighter jets will be used to protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles. The U.K. will also send an Atlas A400M aircraft, used to transport the equipment, as well as military advisers.
“This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks,” Streeting said.
The MoD argued that there is a link between the conflict in the Persian Gulf and the situation domestically in the U.K., pointing to disrupted energy supplies and a subsequent rise in the cost of living.
Since Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street in July he has offered more support to Saudi Arabia. In September, he agreed to a request for air-to-air refueling of the country’s jets.
Pressed Tuesday on whether the U.K. risked being sucked into the Saudi war with the Houthis, Burnham’s official spokesperson told reporters: “I don’t accept that characterization. Our support for Saudi Arabia is considered proportionate and focused on helping them defend themselves against relentless Houthi attacks.”
They added: “Regional instability can have a serious impact at home in the U.K. We’re clear it’s in the U.K.’s economic and security interests that the Houthis do not succeed, and our approach is about defending our people, our interests, and our allies.”

articles.title_orig: Revolut and other banking apps go down as Google Cloud suffers UK outage
articles.title_zh: Revolut and other banking apps go down as Google Cloud suffers UK outage
articles.content_orig:
By SHIVALI BEST, SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY EDITOR
Published: 06:22 EDT, 20 October 2026 | Updated: 12:29 EDT, 20 October 2026
A Google outage has caused hundreds of websites and apps to crash, leaving Britons unable to access NHS services and their online bank accounts.
The tech firm's Cloud service, which provides data storage and processing power for both users and services, began experiencing problems at around 7am today and affected its europe-west2 data centre in London .
Services such as NHS England, Royal Mail and Rightmove went down as a result of the outage , which Google said was due to a power outage.
And several banking apps including Halifax , Lloyds, Revolut and HSBC also experienced issues.
The outage also affected legal proceedings, with the Criminal Bar Association (CBA) saying that it had 'hampered' barristers' attempts to clear the backlog in the courts.
The Russell Brand trial was also affected by the disruption, with some watching the proceedings online unable to access the footage.
In a statement made earlier today, Google claimed that the outage was triggered by a 'a power event'.
However, the tech firm says it has now resolved the issue, writing in a statement that the problem 'has been mitigated for most of the customers and it is believed to be affecting currently a very small number of customers'.
At the time of the outage Google issued an apology to anyone affected by the disruption and thanked users for their 'patience while we're working on resolving the issue'.
A huge outage has hit hundreds of websites and apps due to an issue with the Google Cloud service
According to Down Detector, which tracks service outages, sites experiencing issues include Rightmove, Halifax, Lloyds Bank, Revolut, HSBC, and Royal Mail
According to the Criminal Bar Association (CBA), the outage has 'hampered' barristers' efforts to clear the court backlogs
The outage appears to have caused disruption for a wide range of websites, potentially affecting millions of users
Google Cloud is part of the hidden backbone of the internet that makes many of the services you use every day possible.
Google operates a series of massive data centres containing thousands of computer servers, which companies can rent out for a fee.
These machines process information, handle data analysis, run AI models, and operate internet services via the network of fibre-optic cables that cover the globe.
This allows companies to borrow digital processing power rather than buying and maintaining their own expensive equipment.
That is a lot more efficient, but it means that, if something goes wrong with Google's physical infrastructure, lots of companies can be affected at once.
In a post on X, the CBA wrote: 'Cloud Video Platform (CVP) is down across large parts of England and Wales since 10am.
'Many of us today, both as prosecution and defence counsel, can not proceed with trials and other hearings. Our work to clear backlogs is hampered.'
Likewise, HM Courts and Tribunals Service wrote on X: 'We're aware of an issue affecting Cloud Video Platform, used for some remote hearings.'
Some Britons were also unable to use their online banking services, leaving them unable to send or receive payments.
By 9.00am, online tracker Down Detector showed 480 user-submitted reports of disruption affecting the Lloyds Bank app and website.
Of those affected customers, 36 per cent said they were unable to log in, 31 per cent said they could not use online banking and a further 25 per cent said they could not use the app.
Halifax Bank wrote on X that the company was 'aware some customers are having issues with our app and online'.
The budgeting app Emma reassured customers on social media that the outage was 'not a security issue'.
The company wrote: 'Emma is currently down due to a Google Cloud outage affecting services in London since 7am.'
The banking app Revolut also appeared to be partially affected, with customers worldwide unable to open the app, send money, or even make card payments.
On X, one frustrated customer complained: 'This morning: Can't buy breakfast. Car is stuck in a paid car park. Can't pay for taxi or scooter as backup. Probably should be carrying some cash.'
'Nothing like being stuck in the middle of a city in Japan, unable to pay for literally anything and having to cancel my beauty appointments because my bank @Revolut is having a massive outage,' wrote another.
While one customer said: 'I'm at a petrol station in Australia. Can't pay for my fuel that I just put in my car.. so I'm just standing in the petrol station highly embarrassed and can't get home to my kids.'
Should the NHS and courts rely less on major cloud providers?
The banking app Revolut also appeared to be partially affected, with customers worldwide unable to open the app, send money, or even make card payments
Just like a shipping company might use warehouses as hubs for a certain area, Google Cloud assigns certain data centres to cover specific regions.
A 'region' is a specific geographic area served by a network of data centres, while a 'zone' is an individual location within that area.
The zones are all connected by very fast fibre-optic networks, but are kept separate in case an error ever brings one zone down.
Europe-west2 is the region which includes all of the data centres in and around London, and it is made up of three zones: Europe-west2-a, Europe-west2-b, and Europe-west2-c.
Google doesn't publish the exact boundaries of its individual cloud zones, but we know that Europe-west2-b is in or around London.
Companies that use data centres in multiple zones won't be affected so badly, but companies that are entirely reliant on infrastructure in Europe-west2-b will see more serious outages.
According to Down Detector, issues began around 8.00am this morning and quickly escalated as users shared hundreds of outage reports.
By 8.02am, Revolut had more than 1,458 reports of service disruption.
Of those, 62 per cent of customers said they were having problems with the app, 22 per cent with funds transfer, and 9 per cent with mobile banking.
In a post shared on X earlier today, Revolut says: 'We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers' money and data are safe.
'We've been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.'
Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN, told the Daily Mail: 'When a cloud outage leaves people unable to make payments or access everyday services, it exposes how much we depend on infrastructure we never see.
'For everyday Google users, this dependence can mean several services they rely on suddenly being unavailable at the same time. Someone unable to pay through one banking app may find their alternative is affected too.'
Mr Briedis adds that the enormous scope of Google's cloud computing services means that outages might affect businesses whose customers have no idea they depend on the company at all.
Cloud computing involves companies paying providers such as Google and Amazon to handle their data management, storage and networking at large data centres.
Banking app Revolut's status page shows that services ranging from card payments and ATM withdrawals to stock trading are currently unavailable
By 8.02am, Revolut had over 1,458 reports of service disruption. Of those, 62 per cent of customers said they were having problems with the app, 22 per cent with funds transfer, and nine per cent with mobile banking
These services are typically far cheaper for companies than managing their own servers, and typically extremely reliable.
However, when a major provider does experience a problem, it can have cascading effects due to the number of companies affected.
This outage is the latest in a string of serious service disruptions that have affected cloud services over the last few years.

articles.title_orig: As Politicians Argue About China, US Patients Find Cutting-Edge Treatment There
articles.title_zh: As Politicians Argue About China, US Patients Find Cutting-Edge Treatment There
articles.content_orig:
Until recently, a Manhattanite might venture no more than a few dozen blocks to find the world’s most sophisticated cancer treatment. Cutting-edge American medicines have helped reduce the U.S. cancer death rate by about a third since 1990, and New York City hospitals deliver some of the best care in the country.
But in January 2025, the city’s health systems had no good options for Debbie Doppelt, a 60-year-old jeweler with an unusual form of lung cancer that mostly afflicts nonsmokers like her. The Food and Drug Administration hadn’t yet approved sunvozertinib, a drug developed in China that targets the mutation driving Doppelt’s tumors. She had been through chemotherapy and surgery, but the cancer had now spread to her brain. And she didn’t qualify for the relevant clinical trials.
Then an option emerged, in an offhand remark.
“Too bad she’s not Chinese,” a doctor told her son Max Doppelt, who had organized his mother’s care since her 2023 diagnosis. “She could go to a pharmacy in China and buy it.”
Within hours, mother and son had reached out to friends and relatives, one of whom procured a small supply of sunvozertinib from a contact living in China. A few months later, Max flew to Shanghai to get a refill.
Other patients have followed. “No organization or doctor is guiding patients to China, but word gets out,” Max said. He said he knows of at least 30 Americans who’ve made the pilgrimage to obtain the drug, which the FDA licensed in July 2025 but wasn’t yet on the U.S. market as of mid-October of this year.
Sunvozertinib, made by Shanghai-based Dizal Pharmaceutical, isn’t the only treatment drawing patients to China. Americans, Europeans, and others are trekking there to enter clinical trials for CAR-T therapy, an area in which China is now a world leader .
China, until recently known more as a supplier of drug precursor chemicals and generic medicines, has become a biotech powerhouse, accounting for as much as 46% of new drugs tested around the world in 2025. U.S. pharmaceutical companies are testing new therapies there and signing billion-dollar contracts with Chinese firms to develop and market their drugs.
China’s progress has alarmed some politicians, who warn of lost jobs and U.S. dependency on Chinese medicines. The Trump administration in June kicked off Operation TrialBlazer, aimed at speeding up some FDA regulatory processes to lure back more clinical trials.
China’s poor showing in vaccine and drug development during the covid pandemic prompted the country to overhaul its biotech sector, dramatically altering the global industry, said Sam Rasty, a veteran of small biotech companies who now leads one called FynderBio. Venture capital now flows heavily to early-stage clinical work in China and Australia, where regulatory systems enable key first-in-human studies much more quickly than in the United States.
Chinese companies are so much faster at this process that U.S. biotechs, which used to share early advances at conferences or funding meetings, now routinely conceal their progress out of fear that competitors will take their ideas and speed them to market, said Steve Potts, CEO of Breakthru Medicine, a small biotech.
At a meeting he attended in May, nearly all the 60 biotech CEOs in the room planned to run phase 1 trials in Australia, Europe, or China, Potts said. Five or 10 years ago, most of those trials would have been carried out in the U.S.
“Slow and prohibitive” FDA requirements are driving investment to more-nimble Chinese companies, President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the agency, Heidi Overton, warned in her opening statement at her Sept. 24 confirmation hearing.
The movement of clinical trials overseas “should give pause to every American and those who serve on their behalf,” Overton said. “When we lose this advantage, we lose our health security. And when we lose our health security, we lose everything.”
Overton pledged to continue TrialBlazer, which mirrors Australian processes begun in 1991. It is aimed at accelerating clinical trials and approvals so patients do not feel compelled to seek treatment abroad, said Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson Emily Hilliard. It is sometimes legal to obtain medication abroad for personal use, but the FDA “cautions patients about potential safety and quality risks associated with treatments outside our regulatory system,” she added.
As the FDA moves to streamline drug development, members of Congress are trying to slow Chinese firms’ integration into U.S. biotech.
Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), who chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, in June co-sponsored legislation with Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) requiring all U.S. pharmaceutical deals with Chinese companies to be cleared by the Treasury Department.
Others see biotech protectionism as misguided. China’s focus on improved medicines can only help us, said Peter Kolchinsky, managing partner of RA Capital Management, which has Chinese investments in its biotech portfolio.
“We may be adversaries in many areas, but we’re not competing with them to cure cancer. We are collaborating with them to cure cancer,” he said. “There are things that are bigger enemies than any other nation on Earth.”
Subscribe to KFF Health News' free Morning Briefing.
Cancer Knows No Boundaries
A minor but persistent cough led to the diagnosis of Debbie Doppelt’s cancer in late 2023. Chemo, immunotherapy, and surgery kept it at bay for months, but in December 2024, scans showed the cancer had spread to her brain, with 10 tiny tumors.
The FDA earlier that year had approved amivantamab, a drug that targeted the mutation driving Doppelt’s tumor, but Max was concerned about its toxicity. Also, several doctors he consulted told him that amivantamab might not penetrate brain tissue to fight cancer there.
Doppelt tried to enter a clinical trial at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, where she was a patient, for zipalertinib, another drug that targeted her mutation. But in January 2025, the Doppelts learned that a slight scarring on her lungs had rendered her ineligible for the study.
That left sunvozertinib, which gained approval in China in 2023. It was also being tested in the U.S., but only in late-stage trials in which half the subjects received chemotherapy only. That risk was a nonstarter for Doppelt, whose cancer had already outsmarted chemo.
So Max flew to Shanghai, returning with 26 boxes of sunvozertinib in his luggage. The drugs cost about $10,000, he said.
“Getting on the plane and bringing the medicine home felt like my life’s purpose,” Max said. “The data was so clear that this drug had significant efficacy in the brain. Anything else she might do, she might not last a year.”
On Sept. 1 of this year, AstraZeneca signed an agreement with Dizal to distribute the drug worldwide, and it plans to make it available in the U.S. by the start of 2027, spokesperson Tara Parsell said.
Doppelt, who runs a diamond business with her husband, has tried to stay positive and healthy, scarcely missing a day of work since her 2023 diagnosis. She said she’s grateful she has a loving community and the means to afford the best available therapies.
“I think I’ve been pretty successful at having, actually, an amazing three years,” she said. “In some ways a better three years, with all of it, than the three years before, because you’re so appreciative of everything.”
Doppelt’s parents were Holocaust survivors. “They were always saying: ‘This piece of bread tastes so good! Do you know what it is to be hungry?’”
Searching for help for his mother gave Max, a 30-year-old computer engineer, an idea for helping patients find the right treatment — which, in cases of advanced cancers, may be a clinical trial.
A year ago, he quit his tech job and started a company that uses artificial intelligence to combine data from research and drug company sites with a patient’s health records to help them find the right study.

articles.title_orig: US bans govt agencies from using DeepSeek, China vows to protect firms
articles.title_zh: US bans govt agencies from using DeepSeek, China vows to protect firms
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from civilian U.S. government agencies, citing security concerns.
The Department of Homeland Security on Monday made public the order requiring federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek-related technology from their IT systems and barring them from procuring DeepSeek products and services. The ban applies to federal civilian agency IT systems, including third-party products and services developed using the company's technology.
The move comes amid intensifying geopolitical tensions between Washington and Beijing, with artificial intelligence emerging as a key battleground in the two countries' race for technological dominance.
Asked about the U.S. move by Reuters, China's foreign ministry told the news agency that it would safeguard the rights and interests of its companies.
Mao Ning, a ministry spokesperson, said that "China consistently opposes the over-generalization of national security as well as the politicization of science, technology and trade issues," the agency reported.
The order, originally issued on July 24, applies to federal civilian agencies, including the Treasury, State and Justice departments, but it excludes the Department of Defense.
Since DeepSeek burst onto the scene at the start of 2025, several U.S. government agencies have imposed various restrictions.
Congress restricted the use of DeepSeek in intelligence community systems in December 2025. Earlier that year in March, U.S. Commerce Department bureaus told staff DeepSeek was banned on government devices, Reuters reported at the time. The Defense Information Systems Agency moved to block access to DeepSeek models in January 2025, according to reports from Bloomberg.
DeepSeek's AI models "present multiple threat vectors," the latest DHS order states, citing concerns over potential access to sensitive data by Chinese authorities and potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
The agency also warned that using DeepSeek's AI models could result in sensitive U.S. government data being transferred to China, potentially providing intelligence on American citizens and government programs.
The models may also contain malware or other security vulnerabilities, the agency said, citing open-source research that identified multiple critical vulnerabilities in DeepSeek's iOS app.
Executive agencies can request exceptions to the order, including delays in compliance, by submitting a written justification to the DHS within 60 days of the order's issuance.
DeepSeek and China's Embassy in the U.K. did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
